questions.question: The images show stages of meiosis in the order in which they occur. Which statement is correct?
options: During the stage in image 12, crossing over occurs.
After the stage in image 12, cells are haploid.
During the stage in image 11, DNA will be replicated.
Homologous chromosomes pair up in the stage in image 2.
questions.answer: **1.** By image 12 the first meiotic division is being completed, so the cells that result are haploid.

questions.question: A polypeptide contains the sequence – Asn – Gly – Pro –. Using the mRNA codon table, which DNA template sequence could code for it?
options: TTG / GTT / GGT
TTU / CCC / GGT
UUG / CCC / GGU
TTG / CCC / GGT
questions.answer: **3.** Template TTG CCC GGT transcribes to mRNA AAC GGG CCA, which is Asn–Gly–Pro.

questions.question:
Pea pods can be inflated or constricted, and yellow or green. Experiment 1: homozygous inflated × homozygous constricted. Experiment 2: homozygous yellow × homozygous green. In each, the F1 were crossed among themselves, giving these F2 results:

| Shape | Number | Colour | Number |
|---|---|---|---|
| inflated | 882 | yellow | 152 |
| constricted | 299 | green | 428 |

Based on the data, it can be stated that
options: further crosses are required to determine the inheritance of pod colour.
inflated pod shape is dominant to constricted pod shape.
pod colour and shape are co-dominant characteristics.
green pod colour is recessive to yellow pod colour.
questions.answer: **1.** Inflated : constricted is about 3 : 1, so inflated is dominant (and green, not yellow, is dominant for colour).

questions.question: In pea plants, W (purple) is dominant to w (white). Using the diagram, what are the frequencies of allele W in the original generation and of allele w in the new generation?
questions.answer: **0.** Counting alleles among 9 plants (18 alleles) gives 13 W originally and 10 w in the new generation.

questions.question: The pedigree shows an inherited trait. What is its mode of inheritance?
options: X-linked dominant
X-linked recessive
Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
questions.answer: **3.** Unaffected II-5 and II-6 have an affected child, so it is recessive. II-2 is an affected daughter of an unaffected father, so it cannot be X-linked.

questions.question: Which is true of a somatic mutation?
options: It is not passed on to offspring.
It is a mutation in sex cells.
It is present in all cells of the organism.
It only occurs in one type of cell in the body.
questions.answer: **0.** Somatic mutations occur in body cells, which do not form gametes.

questions.question: Genetic screening has led some people to decide not to have children. This decision will
options: alter the frequency of an allele and therefore affect future human evolution.
have no impact on evolution since DNA is not altered by testing.
increase genetic variation and therefore affect evolution.
result in complete loss of an allele from the population.
questions.answer: **0.** If carriers do not reproduce, their alleles are not passed on, changing allele frequencies.

questions.question: In artificial insemination, sperm from a selected male is used to fertilise many females. What is the main advantage to farmers?
options: It increases genetic diversity in the species.
It allows production of offspring with desired characteristics.
It ensures all offspring are identical to the male.
It produces more vigorous offspring by mixing sperm from several males.
questions.answer: **1.** The farmer can select the male for desirable traits and spread them widely.

questions.question: Which is true of mutations in coding DNA?
options: They can affect the type or sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
They are always neutral.
They check the order of amino acids in a polypeptide.
They have no effect on amino acids.
questions.answer: **0.** Coding DNA specifies amino acid sequence.

questions.question: Fertilisation leads to genetic variation. One way to explain this is:
options: Fertilisation is not a random combination of gametes.
Fertilisation brings somatic cells together.
Fertilisation combines gametes with the same alleles.
Fertilisation combines gametes carrying a variety of alleles for a gene.
questions.answer: **3.** Gametes carry different alleles, so random fusion gives new combinations.

questions.question: Amoxicillin prevents synthesis of bacterial cell walls. Amoxicillin is:
options: a vaccine
an antibiotic
an antiviral drug
a DNA polymerase
questions.answer: **1.** A drug acting against bacteria is an antibiotic.

questions.question: Which is an example of a non-specific immune response?
options: Production of memory T cells
Phagocytes engulfing non-self material
Cloning of B cells to produce plasma cells
Cytotoxic T cells releasing chemicals into infected cells
questions.answer: **1.** Phagocytosis is part of innate immunity.

questions.question: Which is an example of quarantine used to control the spread of disease?
options: Sterilising all food products before packaging
Installing hand sanitisers in commercial kitchens
Removing all fruit from cars entering disease-free orchards
Killing weeds in infested forests
questions.answer: **2.** Quarantine restricts the movement of material that may carry pathogens into a disease-free area.

questions.question: Dengue fever is contracted in Australia only in north Queensland; cases elsewhere are in returning travellers. What best explains the lack of new infections in southern states?
options: Widespread use of antibiotics
Lack of the mosquito vector in southern states
Colder weather inactivates the pathogen
Higher population densities in southern states
questions.answer: **1.** Without the vector mosquito the virus cannot be transmitted.

questions.question: The diagram shows a neurone. The structure labelled X is the:
options: synapse
cell body
myelin sheath
axon terminal

options: stimulus, receptor, effector, control centre, response
stimulus, effector, receptor, control centre, response
stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response
stimulus, control centre, receptor, effector, response
questions.answer: **2.** Receptors detect, the control centre coordinates, effectors respond.

questions.question: A chemical released at the axon terminal crosses the synapse to continue the impulse. It is best described as a:
options: protein
hormone
sodium channel
neurotransmitter
questions.answer: **3.** Chemicals carrying signals across synapses are neurotransmitters.

options: Kidney: osmoregulation and sodium production
Liver: removes toxic wastes and makes lymphocytes
Lung: osmoregulation and removes toxic wastes
Kidney: osmoregulation and removes toxic wastes
questions.answer: **3.** The kidney regulates water and salt balance and removes nitrogenous wastes.

questions.question:
Two cell types were immersed in a protein solution at two temperatures, and the percentage of protein taken up was recorded:

| Time (min) | Type 1, 25°C | Type 1, 37°C | Type 2, 25°C | Type 2, 37°C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 2 | 5 | 5 | 10 |
| 4 | 4 | 10 | 10 | 20 |
| 6 | 6 | 12 | 12 | 24 |
| 8 | 8 | 16 | 16 | 32 |
| 10 | 8 | 16 | 18 | 36 |

Which conclusion is supported by the data?
options: Uptake at 25°C is not affected by cell type.
Uptake by cell type 2 is faster at 37°C than at 25°C.
Uptake by cell type 1 is not affected by temperature.
After another 10 minutes, uptake by cell type 1 would increase.
questions.answer: **1.** At every time, type 2 takes up twice as much at 37°C as at 25°C.

questions.question: The graph shows the average monthly notification rate per 100 000 of illness caused by *Salmonella anatum* in Queensland over five years. It can be concluded that:
options: notifications were highest in May.
the notification rate was fairly steady.
the rate was always lowest in September.
there were four periods with a rate above six per 100 000.
questions.answer: **3.** The rate exceeded 6 in four separate peaks (early 2000, early 2002, mid 2003, early 2004).

questions.question: Contrast features of internal and external fertilisation.
questions.answer:
| Feature | External | Internal |
|---|---|---|
| Site | outside the body, in water | inside the female reproductive tract |
| Gametes | very many eggs and sperm | far fewer eggs |

questions.question: Explain why internal fertilisation is needed for colonising land but is not necessary for life in water.
questions.answer: On land, gametes released into the environment would dry out, and sperm need a liquid in which to swim. Internal fertilisation keeps gametes in a moist, protected environment. In water, gametes can be released directly without drying out and sperm can swim to eggs.

questions.question: Identify the hormone that plays a key role in childbirth in humans.
questions.answer: **Oxytocin**.

questions.question: Describe the role of oxytocin in childbirth.
questions.answer: Oxytocin stimulates contractions of the uterus and the release of prostaglandins (which help soften the cervix and strengthen contractions). Stretching of the cervix triggers more oxytocin (positive feedback) until the baby is born.

questions.question: Draw a fully labelled section of DNA that includes three matched base pairs, and circle a single nucleotide.
questions.answer: Two antiparallel sugar–phosphate backbones joined by complementary base pairs (A–T, G–C) held by hydrogen bonds, with a key; a nucleotide is one phosphate, one deoxyribose and one base (see diagram).

questions.question: The diagram models DNA replication. Explain why it is important for DNA to be replicated as accurately as possible.
questions.answer:
- Each daughter cell (and, via gametes, each offspring) must receive the same genetic information, maintaining heredity and normal cell function.
- DNA codes for polypeptides. An error can change the base sequence, so the amino acid sequence and protein shape change; for example a faulty enzyme would disrupt metabolism.
- Errors become permanent mutations passed to all descendant cells, which may cause disease such as cancer.

questions.question: Identify a transgenic species and state its use.
questions.answer: **Bt cotton:** carries a gene from *Bacillus thuringiensis* so it makes its own insecticidal protein, protecting it against bollworm and reducing pesticide spraying.

questions.question: Describe ONE process used to produce a transgenic species.
questions.answer:
Using *Agrobacterium* for Bt cotton:
1. The Bt toxin gene is cut from bacterial DNA with a restriction enzyme.
2. A plasmid (Ti plasmid) is cut with the same enzyme and the gene joined in with DNA ligase, forming recombinant DNA.
3. The plasmid is put into *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*, which infects plant cells and transfers the gene into their genome.
4. Transformed cells are selected and grown by tissue culture into whole plants, which pass on the gene.

questions.question: Discuss two ethical issues arising from the use of Bt cotton, a transgenic species.
questions.answer:
**1. Environmental and health effects.** *For:* less spraying means less harm to non-target insects and less pesticide exposure for farmers. *Against:* pests may evolve resistance, genes may spread to related plants, and long-term ecological and health effects (e.g. of cottonseed products) are not fully known.

**2. Equity and ownership.** *For:* higher yields can raise income and food and fibre security. *Against:* seed is patented and expensive, so poorer farmers and countries may be excluded or become dependent on a few companies.

questions.question: Draw up a table to compare the causes and effects of point mutations and chromosomal mutations.
questions.answer:
| | Point mutation | Chromosomal mutation |
|---|---|---|
| Change | one or a few bases substituted, inserted or deleted | large segment or whole chromosome deleted, duplicated, inverted, translocated, or number changed |
| Causes | DNA replication errors; mutagens (UV, chemicals) | chromosome breakage (e.g. ionising radiation); non-disjunction or errors in crossing over in meiosis |
| Effects | may be silent, or change one amino acid or the reading frame of one gene, e.g. sickle cell anaemia | affects many genes, usually with major effects, e.g. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) |

questions.question: Mycotoxins are toxic chemicals produced by fungi such as black mould. Some are mutagens that chemically bond to DNA and can lead to cancer. Explain how a mycotoxin mutagen could cause permanent damage to DNA.
questions.answer:
- The chemical binds to a base, distorting the DNA.
- During replication, DNA polymerase cannot recognise the altered base correctly, so the wrong base (or an extra or missing base) is placed in the new strand.
- Repair enzymes remove most damage, but if it is missed, the change is copied in all later replications and becomes a permanent mutation, possibly altering proteins or causing cancer.

questions.question: From an investigation of plant pathogens, name an Australian plant affected by a pathogen, the type of pathogen and the evidence that the pathogen is present.
questions.answer:
- **Plant:** lemon myrtle (*Backhousia citriodora*)
- **Pathogen:** a fungus (myrtle rust, *Austropuccinia psidii*)
- **Evidence:** bright yellow powdery spore pustules on young leaves and shoots, leaf distortion and dieback.

questions.question: Explain the impact of a named plant disease on agricultural production.
questions.answer: **Panama disease of bananas** is caused by a soil fungus (*Fusarium oxysporum*). It invades the roots and blocks the xylem, so plants wilt and die and yield falls. Spores persist in soil for decades and spread on machinery and boots, so infected land may be unusable for susceptible bananas. Farmers lose income and pay for quarantine and destruction of plants, supply falls and prices rise.
Columns with years on the x-axis, deaths per 100 000 on the y-axis, even scale, labels and title (see graph).

questions.question:
Deaths from polio in Australia (a vaccine became available in 1955):

| Years | Deaths per 100 000 |
|---|---|
| 1926–1935 | 6.5 |
| 1936–1945 | 6.8 |
| 1946–1955 | 11.8 |
| 1956–1965 | 1.1 |
| 1966–1975 | 0.1 |

Outline the trends in the data.
questions.answer: Death rates were high and rose to a peak of 11.8 per 100 000 in 1946–1955. After the 1955 vaccine they fell sharply (to 1.1, then 0.1), reaching zero from 1986.

questions.question: Discuss how the work of Robert Koch can be used to identify the cause of an infectious bacterial disease.
questions.answer:
Koch's postulates link a specific microorganism to a specific disease:
1. The microorganism is found in every host with the disease (and not in healthy hosts).
2. It is isolated and grown in pure culture.
3. Inoculating a healthy, susceptible host with the culture produces the same disease.
4. The same microorganism is re-isolated from that host.

They give a rigorous method for establishing the cause. Limitations: some pathogens (e.g. viruses, some bacteria) cannot be cultured on media, some hosts carry a pathogen without symptoms, and testing on humans is unethical.

questions.question: Plants have structures to reduce water loss in hot, dry conditions. Describe TWO such structures and how they assist in water balance.
questions.answer:
- **Sunken stomata** (in pits, often with hairs): humid air is trapped around the pore, reducing the water vapour concentration gradient and so transpiration.
- **Thick waxy cuticle:** a waterproof layer that reduces evaporation from the leaf surface (and reflects some heat).

(Other examples: small or needle leaves reducing surface area; vertically hanging leaves reducing midday heating.)

questions.question: In an experiment, 50 people lay still while the room temperature was lowered from 25°C. Their mean body temperature at the start was 37.1°C. As the room cooled they all shivered, and shivering stopped when the room returned to 25°C. A control group kept at 25°C showed no changes. Draw and label a model of the feedback mechanism that explains these observations.
questions.answer: A negative feedback loop: stimulus → receptors → hypothalamus → muscles → shivering generates heat, counteracting the fall (see diagram).

questions.question: Draw up a table identifying one behavioural, one structural and one physiological adaptation of a named endotherm for maintaining homeostasis in a hot, dry environment.
questions.answer:

|---|---|

questions.question: Sketch a graph of a typical action potential (membrane potential in mV against time) and label the threshold, depolarisation, repolarisation and resting membrane potential.
questions.answer: Resting potential ≈ −70 mV; threshold ≈ −55 mV; rapid rise to about +30 mV (depolarisation); fall back (repolarisation), with a brief undershoot (see graph).

questions.question: Explain why not all stimuli generate an action potential.
questions.answer: An action potential occurs only if the stimulus depolarises the membrane to the threshold (about −55 mV, roughly 15 mV above the −70 mV resting potential). Only then do enough voltage-gated sodium channels open. Weaker (subthreshold) stimuli produce no impulse (all-or-none response).

questions.question:
Maternal and neonatal tetanus claimed about 180 000 lives worldwide in 2002. Graph 1 shows neonatal tetanus deaths and 2-dose vaccine coverage in developing countries (years with no column have no data). Graph 2 shows the antibody response to tetanus vaccine doses from birth to early adulthood.

Evaluate the impact of vaccination on the prevention of disease. Include a description of the body's response to immunisation, and refer to the data.
questions.answer:
**Response to immunisation.** The vaccine (tetanus toxoid) introduces a harmless antigen. Macrophages and dendritic cells engulf it and present it to helper T cells in lymph nodes. Helper T cells release cytokines that activate B cells with matching receptors; these clone into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies, and memory B cells (and memory T cells). On later exposure, memory cells produce antibodies faster and in greater amounts.

**Data.**
- Graph 2: the first dose gives little antibody and not lasting immunity; each later dose produces a faster, higher peak (from below 0.01 IU/mL to over 10 IU/mL), and after five doses levels stay well above the immunity threshold. Without boosters, levels would fall to non-immune, so boosters are essential.
- Graph 1: as coverage rose from under 10% (1980) to about 50% (2000s), estimated deaths fell from about 1.3 million to under 200 000.

**Evaluation.** Vaccination is highly effective: it prevents disease in individuals, protects newborns through maternal antibodies, and for transmissible diseases can give herd immunity and even eradication (smallpox). Its impact is limited by incomplete coverage, cost, access and the need for several doses; for tetanus (caught from soil, not people) there is no herd immunity, and other factors such as hygienic births also reduce deaths. Overall it has had a very large positive impact.

questions.question: Renal dialysis is an effective technology to treat people with kidney disease. The treatment requires a biological understanding of how the kidneys work. Justify this statement.
questions.answer:
**Kidney function.** The kidneys remove nitrogenous waste (urea) and regulate water, salt and pH. In each nephron:
- **Filtration:** high pressure in the glomerulus forces water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea into Bowman's capsule; cells and large proteins stay in the blood.
- **Reabsorption:** glucose and amino acids are actively reabsorbed in the proximal tubule; salts and water are reabsorbed there, in the loop of Henle and collecting duct (under ADH and aldosterone control).
- **Secretion:** H⁺, K⁺ and some drugs are secreted into the tubule.

**How dialysis applies this.**
- Blood flows past a semipermeable membrane that, like the glomerulus, retains cells and proteins while small molecules cross.
- Urea diffuses into the dialysate, which contains none, and the dialysate is continually replaced to keep the gradient.
- Instead of active reabsorption, the dialysate contains glucose and ions at normal blood levels, so there is no net loss of what the body needs, while excess ions diffuse out.
- Excess water is removed by adjusting pressure; countercurrent flow improves exchange.

**Judgement.** The statement is justified: knowing what the nephron removes and retains determines the membrane and dialysate design. Dialysis is effective at sustaining life, but it is intermittent, time-consuming and does not replace hormonal functions, so it is less effective than a healthy kidney or transplant.

questions.question: *Salmonella enterica* causes food poisoning. In 2006 scientists sent a batch of salmonella to space and kept an identical batch on Earth at similar temperatures. Bacteria from both were fed to mice, and the 'space germs' were reported to be three times more likely to make the mice sick. Outline a safety procedure the scientists could use to minimise their risk of infection.
questions.answer: They should wear gloves and a lab coat, and wash their hands and disinfect work surfaces after handling the cultures, so that bacteria cannot be transferred to their mouths.

questions.question: *Salmonella enterica* causes food poisoning. In 2006 scientists sent a batch of salmonella to space and kept an identical batch on Earth at similar temperatures. Bacteria from both were fed to mice, and the 'space germs' were reported to be three times more likely to make the mice sick. Outline and justify TWO steps the scientists could include to increase the validity of their method.
questions.answer:
1. **Use the same strain and the same dose of bacteria for both groups of mice.** Then the only difference between the bacteria is whether they went to space, so a difference in illness can be attributed to that variable.
2. **Use mice of the same species, age, sex and health, kept under the same conditions with the same diet.** This controls other factors that affect susceptibility, so they cannot explain the result.

(Also acceptable: a control group fed sterile food; the same time between feeding and assessing illness.)

questions.question: Discuss the role of quarantine in preventing the spread of disease, using a specific example.
questions.answer:
Quarantine restricts the movement of people, animals, plants or goods that may carry a pathogen, until they are shown to be free of it. This breaks the chain of transmission.

**Example:** during the COVID-19 pandemic, overseas arrivals to Australia spent 14 days in hotel quarantine. This identified many infected travellers before they could mix with the community and greatly slowed spread.

**Limitations:** it is costly, restricts freedom and is only as good as its enforcement; leaks from hotel quarantine in Melbourne in 2020 led to a large outbreak. It is therefore highly effective as one measure, combined with testing and contact tracing.

*Note: the school's example is fruit fly, which is a crop pest rather than a disease.*

questions.question: In 2013 researchers reported a child with mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, caused by a mutation in the anticodon region of the tRNA for the amino acid tryptophan. The disease causes stroke-like symptoms and affects all major organs. Using your knowledge of the role of tRNA, discuss the potential impact of this mutation on normal cell function.
questions.answer:
In polypeptide synthesis, DNA is transcribed into mRNA, whose codons are read by ribosomes. Each tRNA carries a particular amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with a complementary mRNA codon, so amino acids are joined in the correct order.

A mutation in the anticodon of the tryptophan tRNA may stop it binding to the tryptophan codon, so tryptophan is not added and the chain may stall or be left incomplete. Or it may pair with a different codon, putting tryptophan where another amino acid belongs.

Either way, the primary structure, and therefore folding and function, of many proteins is altered. As this tRNA is used in mitochondria, proteins of cellular respiration would be affected, reducing ATP production. Cells with high energy demands, such as brain and muscle, would be damaged first, which is consistent with symptoms affecting major organs. The severity depends on what proportion of the mitochondria carry the mutation.

questions.question: A female who is heterozygous for a trait reproduces with a male who has the dominant allele. The chance of a daughter showing the dominant trait is 100%, and the chance of a son showing it is 50%. Identify the pattern of inheritance.
questions.answer: Sex-linked (X-linked) inheritance, with the trait of interest determined by a dominant allele.

questions.question: A female who is heterozygous for a trait reproduces with a male who has the dominant allele. The chance of a daughter showing the dominant trait is 100%, and the chance of a son showing it is 50%. Construct a model to support the pattern of inheritance.
questions.answer:
Cross: $X^DX^d\times X^DY$

| | $X^D$ | $Y$ |
|---|---|---|
| $X^D$ | $X^DX^D$ | $X^DY$ |
| $X^d$ | $X^DX^d$ | $X^dY$ |

Both daughter genotypes include $X^D$, so 100% of daughters show the dominant trait. Of the sons, $X^DY$ shows it and $X^dY$ does not, so the chance is 50%.

questions.question: Two different mutations in a DNA sequence are shown; each may harm the cell or have no impact. Outline the difference between the two mutations.
questions.answer: Mutation I is a point **substitution**: one base, G, is replaced by A, and the sequence length is unchanged. Mutation II is an **insertion**: an extra A is added, which causes a frameshift in the reading of the triplets that follow.

questions.question: Two different mutations in a DNA sequence are shown; each may harm the cell or have no impact. Which mutation is likely to have the greater effect on a cell? Give evidence to support your answer.
questions.answer:
**Mutation II.** The inserted base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after the insertion is read differently. Many amino acids will be wrong and a premature stop codon may appear, probably giving a non-functional protein.

Mutation I changes only one triplet. At most one amino acid changes (or a stop codon is made), and because the genetic code is degenerate it may have no effect at all.

questions.question: Two females of the same age and build ate identical meals. The graph shows their blood glucose levels over the next five hours. Explain whether Emily or Grace has a disorder in blood glucose homeostasis, referring to at least two parts of the graph.
questions.answer:
**Emily.**

1. Her level rises far higher (to about 200 units, compared with about 120 for Grace) and keeps rising until 1 hour, while Grace's peaks at about 30 minutes. This suggests insulin is not being released, or is not acting, quickly enough.
2. Her level falls slowly and is still above its starting value (about 100 compared with 75) after five hours, while Grace's returns to normal. Glucose is not being removed from her blood effectively.

questions.question: Two females of the same age and build ate identical meals. The graph shows their blood glucose levels over the next five hours. Explain the small rise in Grace's blood glucose between four and five hours.
questions.answer:
At about four hours her blood glucose has fallen below the set point. This is detected by the pancreas, which releases glucagon. Glucagon causes the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood, raising the level back towards normal: an example of negative feedback.

*Note: the school says the liver releases glycogen; it releases glucose produced from stored glycogen.*

questions.question: The Tasmanian devil is at risk of extinction from the contagious cancer devil facial tumour disease (DFTD). The cancer spreads because nearly all devils have very similar MHC genes (which allow the immune system to recognise foreign molecules): cancer cells transferred during fights are not recognised as foreign. Suggest why most devils have very similar MHC genes.
questions.answer: The devils are an isolated island population that has been through population bottlenecks, so inbreeding and genetic drift have left very little genetic diversity, including in the MHC genes.

questions.question: The Tasmanian devil is at risk of extinction from the contagious cancer devil facial tumour disease (DFTD). The cancer spreads because nearly all devils have very similar MHC genes (which allow the immune system to recognise foreign molecules): cancer cells transferred during fights are not recognised as foreign. Researchers compared over 90 000 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in pre-infection and post-infection populations and found two genomic regions with immune genes that appear to be under strong selection. Explain the advantages of using SNPs in genetic analyses.
questions.answer:
- SNPs are very **numerous and spread across the whole genome**, so they give detailed coverage and can locate regions linked to a trait such as disease resistance.
- Most lie in non-coding DNA and are not removed by selection, so they are **stable markers of genetic variation** that can be compared between individuals and populations; changes in their frequencies reveal selection.
- Large numbers can be tested **quickly and cheaply** by automated methods, without sequencing entire genomes.

questions.question: Crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) plants, such as pineapple (*Ananas comosus*), absorb carbon dioxide at night and store it as malic acid. During the day the malic acid is converted back to carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. Using your understanding of plant structure and function, explain how this helps pineapple maintain water balance.
questions.answer: Plants must open their stomata to take in carbon dioxide, but water vapour is lost through the open pores by transpiration. CAM plants open their stomata at night, when it is cooler and more humid, so much less water evaporates. In the hot day the stomata stay closed, conserving water, while the stored malic acid supplies carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. This helps the plant survive in hot, dry conditions.

questions.question: Identify and describe a feature or mechanism, other than CAM metabolism, that helps a named plant maintain water balance.
questions.answer: Oleander (*Nerium oleander*) has stomata sunk in hairy pits on the underside of the leaf. The pits trap a layer of humid air next to the stomata, reducing the diffusion gradient for water vapour and so reducing water loss.

questions.question: 'Prevention is better than cure.' Evaluate this statement for infectious diseases by outlining FOUR strategies used to prevent or control their spread.
questions.answer:
1. **Hygiene and sanitation:** hand washing, safe food handling and treating drinking water stop pathogens reaching new hosts, for example preventing cholera. It is cheap and works against many diseases at once.
2. **Vaccination:** antigens stimulate memory B and T cells, so later exposure gives a rapid response before illness develops. With high coverage, herd immunity protects others; smallpox was eradicated this way.
3. **Quarantine and isolation:** restricting the movement of infected or exposed people, animals and goods breaks transmission, for example for COVID-19, or keeping foot-and-mouth disease out of Australia.
4. **Vector control:** insecticides, bed nets and draining standing water reduce mosquitoes and so malaria transmission.

**Evaluation:** the statement is largely valid. Prevention avoids suffering, death and spread, is usually cheaper than treating large numbers of cases, and is the only option where there is no effective cure (many viral diseases). It also reduces antibiotic use and so slows resistance. However, prevention is never complete (not all diseases have vaccines, and measures depend on compliance and resources), so treatments such as antibiotics and antivirals remain essential. The best approach combines both, with prevention as the priority.

questions.question: DNA profiling was used to test the paternity of a child. The banding patterns of the mother, child and three men are shown. Identify which man is most likely to be the father.
questions.answer: George.

questions.question: DNA profiling was used to test the paternity of a child. The banding patterns of the mother, child and three men are shown. Justify your choice of father with reference to the profile.
questions.answer: Every band in the child must come from the mother or the father. Several of the child's bands match the mother; all of the remaining bands are present in George's profile at the same positions. Emmanuel and Simon each match only one or two of them.

questions.question: DNA profiling can also be used to match DNA from a crime scene with that of suspects. Outline the techniques used in DNA profiling.
questions.answer:
1. DNA is extracted from each sample, and the regions to be compared (such as short tandem repeats) are amplified by **PCR** using primers, free nucleotides and DNA polymerase; alternatively the DNA is cut with restriction enzymes.
2. The fragments are separated by **gel electrophoresis**: an electric current moves the negatively charged DNA through the gel, with smaller fragments travelling further.
3. The fragments are made visible and the **banding patterns compared**. A match at all positions indicates the DNA very probably came from the same person.

questions.question: In the humoral response, B cells are activated by antigen and produce many copies of themselves. Describe how the body responds after these steps and explain how this reduces the impact of the pathogen.
questions.answer:
The cloned B cells, stimulated by cytokines from helper T cells, differentiate into:

- **Plasma cells**, which secrete large quantities of antibody specific to the antigen. Antibodies neutralise toxins and viruses, clump pathogens together and mark them for phagocytes, so the pathogen is cleared and does less damage.
- **Memory B cells**, which remain in the body for years. On re-exposure they quickly divide and form plasma cells, giving a faster and larger antibody response that usually destroys the pathogen before symptoms develop.

*Note: the school's answer says some B cells become 'helper B cells'; the long-lived cells are memory B cells.*

questions.question: Construct a table to compare and contrast B cells and T cells.
questions.answer:
| Feature | B cells | T cells |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Made in bone marrow | Made in bone marrow |
| Maturation | Bone marrow | Thymus |
| Specificity | Specific receptors for one antigen | Specific receptors for one antigen |
| Immune response | Humoral (antibody-mediated) | Cell-mediated |
| Antigen recognition | Can bind free antigen | Recognise antigen presented on MHC molecules |
| Cells formed | Plasma cells and memory B cells | Helper, cytotoxic, suppressor and memory T cells |
| Action | Secrete antibodies | Release cytokines; kill infected or abnormal cells |
| Memory | Form memory cells | Form memory cells |

questions.question: Adrian (male) showed signs of a genetic disease and married Betty, who did not. They had three children: Charles (male), David (male) and Ellen (female). Charles and David were genetically healthy, but Ellen may have been a carrier. Ellen married Freddy (male), who did not have the disease. They had two sons: Geoff, who had the disease, and Harry, who was disease-free. Draw a pedigree illustrating this information, showing the conventions used.
questions.answer: Three generations with offspring in birth order; the key gives the symbols. Ellen must be a carrier because Geoff is affected although neither of his parents is.

questions.question: Adrian (male) showed signs of a genetic disease and married Betty, who did not. They had three children: Charles (male), David (male) and Ellen (female). Charles and David were genetically healthy, but Ellen may have been a carrier. Ellen married Freddy (male), who did not have the disease. They had two sons: Geoff, who had the disease, and Harry, who was disease-free. Could this be a sex-linked disorder? Outline reasons for your answer.
questions.answer: Yes, it fits X-linked recessive inheritance. Only males are affected, and it skips a generation, passing from Adrian through his carrier daughter Ellen to his grandson Geoff. Adrian's sons do not carry the allele, as expected since they inherit his Y chromosome, not his X.

questions.question: The diagram shows a section of the human eye. Choose TWO of the lettered parts and, for each, name the structure and give its function.
questions.answer:
| Letter | Structure | Function |
|---|---|---|
| a | Cornea | Transparent front of the eye that refracts light, providing most of the eye's focusing power |
| f | Optic nerve | Carries nerve impulses from the retina to the brain |

questions.question: Alex's optometrist found that his blurry vision is caused by myopia. Distinguish between myopia and hyperopia and outline a technology that can correct Alex's condition.
questions.answer:
In **myopia** (short-sightedness) the eyeball is too long or the cornea/lens too strongly curved, so light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina; near objects are clear but distant ones blurred. In **hyperopia** (long-sightedness) the eyeball is too short or the focusing too weak, so light would focus behind the retina; near objects in particular are blurred.

**Correction:** spectacles with concave (diverging) lenses spread the light rays slightly before they enter the eye, so the image forms on the retina. (Contact lenses or laser surgery to flatten the cornea are alternatives.)

questions.question: A gene has three alleles in a population: G1, G2 and G3. The frequency of G1 is 0.60 and of G2 is 0.25. What is the frequency of G3?

A gene has three alleles in a population: G1, G2 and G3. The frequency of G1 is 0.60 and of G2 is 0.25. A person homozygous for G2 reproduces with a person homozygous for G3. It was stated that they have a 25% chance of producing a child with the G2 trait in their phenotype. Determine the validity of this analysis, with evidence.
questions.answer:
The statement is **not valid**.

- Population allele frequencies (such as 0.25 for G2) do not give the probability for a particular cross; the parents' genotypes do.
- Here the parents are G2G2 and G3G3, so (for an autosomal gene) every child is G2G3. Whether G2 shows then depends on dominance: 100% if G2 is dominant to G3, 0% if it is recessive, and a combined or intermediate phenotype if they are codominant or incompletely dominant.
- The question gives no information on dominance or whether the gene is sex-linked, so the phenotype cannot be predicted, and nothing supports a figure of 25%.

questions.question: Biotechnology has affected Earth's biodiversity for many years, and farmers and scientists used many methods to increase food production before genetic engineering. Outline ONE example of biotechnology from the past, ONE from the present and ONE potential future example. Evaluate their effects on biodiversity.
questions.answer:
**Past: selective breeding.** For thousands of years farmers have chosen plants and animals with desirable traits to breed, producing, for example, high-yielding wheat and dairy cattle. *Effect:* many distinct breeds and varieties were created, but intensive selection narrows each gene pool, and replacing local varieties with a few favoured ones has lost alleles, leaving crops more vulnerable to disease.

**Present: transgenic crops,** such as Bt cotton, which has a bacterial gene for an insecticidal protein. *Effect:* it adds new genetic combinations and greatly reduces insecticide spraying, which helps non-target insects. However, planting few elite lines over large areas reduces genetic diversity, and there are risks of gene flow to wild relatives and of resistant pests evolving.

**Future: gene editing (CRISPR) to make crops tolerant of heat and drought.** *Effect:* higher yields on existing farmland could reduce land clearing, protecting ecosystem diversity, and editing could restore useful alleles to many local varieties. But if a few edited varieties replace others, the crop's genetic diversity would fall further, and unintended ecological effects are possible.

**Evaluation:** biotechnology has increased food production but has often reduced genetic diversity within agricultural species, mainly through the widespread use of uniform varieties rather than the technique itself. Its overall effect can be limited by maintaining seed banks, using many varieties with refuge areas, and monitoring new crops, so the benefit depends on how it is managed.

questions.question: Describe ONE response of a named Australian plant to a named pathogen.
questions.answer:
**Plant:** *Lomandra longifolia* (spiny-headed mat-rush). **Pathogen:** the water mould *Phytophthora cinnamomi*.

When the pathogen invades the roots, cells produce **hydrogen peroxide** (a reactive oxygen species). This is toxic to the pathogen, helps cross-link and strengthen cell walls, and triggers programmed death of cells around the infection, which limits its spread.

questions.answer:

questions.question: For a named non-infectious disease, state its cause, its effects and TWO methods of prevention.
questions.answer:
**Disease:** mesothelioma.

**Cause:** inhaling asbestos fibres, which lodge in the mesothelium around the lungs, causing chronic inflammation and DNA damage.

**Effects:** cancer (uncontrolled cell division) of the mesothelium; chest pain, fluid around the lungs, shortness of breath; usually fatal.

**Prevention 1:** legislation banning the manufacture, import and use of asbestos.

**Prevention 2:** licensed removal with respirators, protective clothing and wetting of material so fibres are not inhaled.

questions.question: Outline the process of translation.
questions.answer:
- mRNA carrying the code from DNA binds to a ribosome in the cytoplasm; translation begins at a start codon.
- tRNA molecules, each carrying a specific amino acid, pair their anticodon with the complementary mRNA codon.
- The ribosome moves along the mRNA, joining amino acids with peptide bonds, until a stop codon releases the completed polypeptide.

questions.question: The table shows the effect of soil temperature on the germination of onion seeds (percentage germinating and days taken to emerge). Graph all of the data.
questions.answer: Temperature (independent variable) on the horizontal axis; two labelled vertical axes with units, one for each data set; points plotted accurately; a smooth curve of best fit for each, distinguished by a key; and a title.

questions.question: The table shows the effect of soil temperature on the germination of onion seeds (percentage germinating and days taken to emerge). Describe the trends shown when the data are graphed.
questions.answer:
- **Germination percentage:** rises from 90% at 0 °C to about 98% from 5–25 °C, then falls, sharply above 30 °C (2% at 40 °C).
- **Days to emerge:** falls steeply from 136 days at 0 °C to a minimum of 4 days at 25–30 °C, then rises to 25 days at 40 °C.

questions.question: The table shows the effect of soil temperature on the germination of onion seeds (percentage germinating and days taken to emerge). With reference to a graph of the data, discuss the optimal temperature for planting onion seeds.
questions.answer: About **20–25 °C**. Germination is at or near its maximum (99% at 20 °C, 97% at 25 °C) and emergence is almost fastest (5 and 4 days). Above 30 °C germination collapses; below 10 °C emergence is very slow.

questions.question: Evaluate the impact of scientific knowledge on the manipulation of plant reproduction in agriculture, using ONE example other than germination temperature.
questions.answer:
**Example: artificial pollination (selective breeding of wheat).**

- **Knowledge:** pollen carries male gametes from anther to stigma, and traits are inherited in predictable ways.
- **Process:** breeders remove the anthers of one parent to stop self-pollination, transfer pollen from a parent with a desired trait (e.g. rust resistance), bag the flower, then select the best offspring over generations. William Farrer used this to produce Federation wheat.
- **Impact:** higher yields, disease resistance and drought tolerance.
- **Limitations:** it is slow, and widespread planting of few varieties reduces genetic diversity.

**Judgement:** the impact has been very large and positive for food production, provided genetic diversity is conserved.

questions.question: Resting heart rate is controlled by pacemaker cells. The sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate and the parasympathetic decreases it. Low arterial oxygen (hypoxia) is detected by chemoreceptors in the carotid body, which signal the cardiorespiratory centre in the medulla oblongata, increasing the sympathetic response. High oxygen (hyperoxia) increases the parasympathetic response. Complete the diagram to show the homeostasis of arterial oxygen levels, identifying stimuli, receptors, effectors and responses.
questions.answer:
**When O₂ increases:** stimulus (raised arterial O₂) → receptor (chemoreceptors in carotid body) → control centre (cardiorespiratory centre in medulla) → parasympathetic nerves → effector (pacemaker cells of the heart) → response (heart rate decreases) → O₂ delivery falls, returning levels to normal.

**When O₂ decreases:** stimulus (lowered arterial O₂) → chemoreceptors → medulla → sympathetic nerves → pacemaker cells → heart rate increases → O₂ delivery rises, returning levels to normal.

Both loops are negative feedback.

questions.question: Resting heart rate is controlled by pacemaker cells. The sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate and the parasympathetic decreases it. Low arterial oxygen (hypoxia) is detected by chemoreceptors in the carotid body, which signal the cardiorespiratory centre in the medulla oblongata, increasing the sympathetic response. High oxygen (hyperoxia) increases the parasympathetic response. Explain why the control of heart rate in response to oxygen levels uses the nervous system rather than the endocrine system.
questions.answer: Abnormal oxygen levels damage tissues quickly, so correction must be immediate and adjustable moment to moment. Nerve impulses act within milliseconds on a specific target and stop quickly; hormones travel in the blood and act more slowly and for longer.

questions.question: Horse coat colour: the MC1R gene has alleles $E$, $e$ and $e^a$ ($e$ and $e^a$ recessive to $E$); horses with $E$ produce black pigment, those without produce only red. The ASIP (Agouti) gene controls black pigment distribution: $A$ restricts it to the points (mane, tail, lower legs), $a$ spreads it over the whole body. Bay, chestnut and black horses are shown. Using this example, explain the meaning of *multiple alleles*.
questions.answer: Alleles are different versions of a gene. A gene has multiple alleles when **more than two** exist in the population, as for MC1R ($E$, $e$, $e^a$), although each horse carries only two.

questions.question: Pneumonia is an infection of the alveoli. In 2017 it was the leading cause of death of children under 5 (over 800,000 deaths, down from over 2 million in 1990). It is spread by droplets but is not highly contagious and is often a consequence of poverty. Just over half of fatal infections were caused by *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, which normally lives harmlessly in the upper respiratory tract but can infect the lower tract if the upper tract is compromised. A vaccine covering several strains is 80% effective against those strains. The graph shows child deaths by risk factor. Explain how a vaccine may prevent infection by *S. pneumoniae*.
questions.answer: The vaccine introduces harmless antigens from the bacterium. B and T cells with matching receptors are activated, multiply, and produce antibodies and **memory cells**. On later exposure, memory cells respond rapidly and strongly, so antibodies neutralise and tag the bacteria for destruction before they establish an infection.

It is spread by droplets but is not highly contagious and is often a consequence of poverty. Just over half of fatal infections were caused by *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, which normally lives harmlessly in the upper respiratory tract but can infect the lower tract if the upper tract is compromised. A vaccine covering several strains is 80% effective against those strains. The graph shows child deaths by risk factor. Using the data, justify THREE public health campaigns, apart from vaccination, that could significantly reduce deaths of children under 5 from pneumonia.
questions.answer:
1. **Child nutrition (including breastfeeding).** Child wasting is by far the largest risk factor (over 400,000 deaths in 2017, about double the next). Educating families about diet and exclusive breastfeeding, monitoring growth and supplying food supplements would strengthen children's immunity and would also reduce stunting, underweight and vitamin A and zinc deficiency.
2. **Clean cooking.** Indoor air pollution from solid fuels is the second largest factor (over 200,000 deaths). Promoting clean stoves and fuels and better ventilation would reduce damage to children's airways.
3. **Handwashing.** Lack of handwashing facilities accounts for roughly 100,000 or more deaths. Providing soap and water and teaching hygiene would reduce transmission of pathogens (and diarrhoeal illness that contributes to wasting).

Targeting the largest factors in poorer regions gives the greatest reduction; since risk factors overlap, the totals cannot simply be added.

questions.question: Describe the use of ONE technology to assist with the effects of a non-infectious disease or disorder.
questions.answer: **Haemodialysis for kidney failure.** Kidneys normally remove wastes such as urea and regulate water and salts. In dialysis, blood is pumped through tubing with a semi-permeable membrane surrounded by dialysate flowing the opposite way. Urea and excess salts and water move out of the blood; the dialysate has ideal levels of glucose and ions so these are not lost. It is done about three times a week for several hours.

questions.question:
Diphtheria study (Andhra Pradesh): patients presented with fever, pharyngitis and a patch in the throat; age, presentation, morbidity, mortality, cultured bacteria and immunisation status were recorded. Of 61 950 admissions from January 2008 to December 2012, 2925 (4.7%) had clinical diphtheria: 1194 immunised and 1731 non-immunised. Immunised patients had milder disease. Culture-positive immunised patients had *Corynebacterium* other than *diphtheriae* (COD, n = 104) or *C. diphtheriae* (CD, n = 23), had mild disease and recovered completely. Culture-positive non-immunised patients had COD (n = 11) or CD (n = 412). 81 patients (3%) died, 77 of them non-immunised, usually of myocarditis; 73% of deaths were in children under 5.

State the type of study and summarise its findings.
questions.answer:
**Type:** descriptive observational study of hospital records (retrospective cohort comparing immunised and non-immunised patients).

**Findings:**
- Immunised patients had milder disease and made up only 4 of the 81 deaths.
- *C. diphtheriae* was far more common in non-immunised patients (412) than immunised patients (23).
- Most deaths (73%) were in children under 5, usually from myocarditis.

questions.question: Influenza A is an RNA virus with a segmented genome (8 segments, at least 10 genes), shown. HA protein binds the virus to cells of the upper respiratory tract, which take it in by endocytosis; replication occurs in the host nucleus using viral RNA polymerase (genes PA, PB1, PB2). New particles bud from the cell with HA and NA in the membrane; NA lets them leave. Infected cells release signalling molecules; dendritic cells present viral antigens to T cells and antibodies are eventually produced. The viral RNA polymerase has no proof-reading, giving a high mutation rate. Outline TWO possible consequences of point mutation in the coding regions.
questions.answer:
1. A missense or nonsense mutation changes or truncates a protein, which may impair the virus (e.g. its ability to enter cells) or alter an antigen so it escapes immunity.
2. A silent mutation still codes for the same amino acid (the code is degenerate), so there is no change to the protein.

questions.question: Influenza A is an RNA virus with a segmented genome (8 segments, at least 10 genes), shown. HA protein binds the virus to cells of the upper respiratory tract, which take it in by endocytosis; replication occurs in the host nucleus using viral RNA polymerase (genes PA, PB1, PB2). New particles bud from the cell with HA and NA in the membrane; NA lets them leave. Infected cells release signalling molecules; dendritic cells present viral antigens to T cells and antibodies are eventually produced. In which genes is point mutation most likely to affect the adaptive immune system's ability to combat the virus on a second infection? Justify.
questions.answer: **HA and NA.** Their proteins are on the virus surface and are the main antigens recognised. The first infection produces antibodies and memory B and T cells specific to their shapes. If mutation changes these shapes, memory cells and antibodies bind poorly, so the secondary response is slower and weaker.

questions.question: Influenza A is an RNA virus with a segmented genome (8 segments, at least 10 genes), shown. HA protein binds the virus to cells of the upper respiratory tract, which take it in by endocytosis; replication occurs in the host nucleus using viral RNA polymerase (genes PA, PB1, PB2). New particles bud from the cell with HA and NA in the membrane; NA lets them leave. Infected cells release signalling molecules; dendritic cells present viral antigens to T cells and antibodies are eventually produced. Co-infection of one cell by different influenza A viruses allows segments to be reassorted (antigenic shift); recombination can also occur. New epidemic strains occasionally form in poultry-farming regions. Propose how this might occur.
questions.answer:
- Large numbers of birds crowded together, in close contact with people (and often pigs), allow bird and human strains of influenza A to circulate in the same place.
- One host cell becomes infected with two different strains.
- During replication, segments from both are packaged into new particles (reassortment), giving a new combination of HA and NA.
- Humans have no immunity to the new subtype, so if it spreads between people an epidemic results.

questions.question: How important is it for genetic material to be replicated exactly? Consider the life cycles of both pathogen and host, using at least TWO infectious diseases you have studied.
questions.answer:
**Accuracy matters for continuity.** DNA or RNA codes for proteins. Before mitosis and meiosis, DNA is copied semi-conservatively, with proof-reading and repair. Errors can produce non-functional proteins; in humans, mutations can cause cancer, and germ-line mutations can cause inherited disorders.

**Pathogens also depend on it.** *Plasmodium* (malaria) must complete a complex cycle through mosquito gut and salivary glands and human liver and red blood cells; harmful errors could disable any stage. Influenza A must copy genes for HA, polymerase and NA correctly to enter cells, replicate and escape.

**But exact copying is not always advantageous.** Influenza's error-prone polymerase causes antigenic drift, letting it evade memory cells, so vaccines must be updated. Mutation in *Plasmodium* has produced resistance to drugs such as chloroquine.

**Hosts also benefit from variation.** B cells deliberately mutate antibody genes (somatic hypermutation), producing higher-affinity antibodies. The sickle-cell allele, which arose by mutation, protects heterozygotes against malaria.

**Judgement:** replication must be accurate enough to keep essential functions, so most of the genome must be copied faithfully; yet a low level of error is essential for populations of both pathogen and host to adapt.

questions.question: Explain how the immune system responds after exposure to a pathogen, referring to innate and adaptive immunity.
questions.answer:
**Innate (rapid, non-specific):** barriers such as skin, mucus, cilia, lysozyme and stomach acid resist entry. If breached, damaged cells release histamine, causing inflammation so more blood and white cells arrive. Phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages) engulf pathogens; fever and complement proteins hinder them.
**Adaptive (slower, specific):** macrophages and dendritic cells present antigens to matching helper T cells, which release cytokines. These activate B cells, which divide into plasma cells (secreting specific antibodies that neutralise and tag pathogens) and memory B cells; and cytotoxic T cells, which destroy infected cells, plus memory T cells.
Memory cells make the response to a second exposure faster and stronger.

questions.question: Map 1 shows diabetes prevalence and Map 2 shows GDP per capita. Analyse the maps to identify patterns, relationships and possible causes of diabetes.
questions.answer:
**Patterns:** the highest prevalence (14–17%) is in parts of North Africa and the Middle East; much of the Americas, Russia and China are 8–11%; the lowest (2–5%) is in much of sub-Saharan Africa. Australia and much of Europe are moderate or low-to-moderate.
**Relationship:** the poorest sub-Saharan countries mostly have low prevalence, while many middle- and high-income countries are higher, but the link is not simple: some very wealthy countries (e.g. Australia) are lower than some middle-income ones.
**Possible causes:** greater income and urbanisation can bring energy-dense diets, inactivity and obesity; genetics, age structure and differences in diagnosis also matter. Correlation alone does not show cause.

questions.question: Outline ONE example of biotechnology from the past, ONE from the present and ONE potential future example, and evaluate the effects of each on biodiversity.
questions.answer:
**Past – selective breeding** (e.g. wheat, dairy cattle): people bred individuals with desired traits. It created many local breeds, but intensive selection narrowed gene pools and replaced wild or traditional varieties, a mostly negative effect on genetic diversity.
**Present – transgenic crops** (e.g. Bt cotton): a bacterial gene gives insect resistance. Less broad-spectrum spraying can protect non-target insects, but large monocultures reduce genetic diversity, resistant pests can evolve and genes may spread. The net effect depends on management.
**Future – gene editing (CRISPR)** of crops for heat tolerance, or of endangered species for disease resistance. It could save species and reduce land clearing through higher yields (positive), but widespread uniform varieties or unintended edits could reduce diversity or disrupt ecosystems.
**Judgement:** past and present technologies have generally narrowed diversity in farmed species; future effects could be positive if regulation, refuges and gene banks maintain variation.

questions.question: The back of the leopard frog can be patterned or non-patterned. Several patterned frogs bred and produced 75 patterned and 25 non-patterned offspring. Which phenotype is dominant? Explain with a Punnett square.
questions.answer:
**Patterned is dominant** (P), non-patterned recessive (p). Patterned parents produced some non-patterned offspring, so the parents must carry a hidden recessive allele: Pp × Pp.

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & P & p\\\hline P & PP & Pp\\ p & Pp & pp\end{array}$$

This gives 3 patterned : 1 non-patterned, matching 75 : 25. (If non-patterned were dominant, patterned parents would be pp and all offspring would be patterned.)

questions.question: Fertilisation can be internal or external. Compare and contrast internal and external fertilisation in terms of (i) chance of fertilisation and (ii) environment for the zygote, giving differences and a similarity for each.
questions.answer:
**Chance of fertilisation**
- External: lower for each gamete, as gametes disperse in water.
- Internal: higher, as gametes are placed close together.
- Similarity: both need male and female gametes to fuse to form a zygote.

**Environment for the zygote**
- External: exposed to a changing environment and predators.
- Internal: develops (at least initially) inside the female, protected and stable.
- Similarity: both require a moist or watery environment so gametes and zygote do not dry out.

questions.question: The diagram shows human blood passing through an artificial kidney (dialyser). Evaluate the effectiveness of dialysis compared with normal kidney function for filtering blood.
questions.answer:
Kidneys filter blood continuously, removing urea by filtration and then selectively reabsorbing water, glucose and ions (by passive and active transport), adjusting to the body's needs.

In dialysis, blood flows past a semipermeable membrane bathed in dialysate containing glucose and ions at normal levels but no urea. Urea and excess ions diffuse out; blood cells and proteins are retained. Only passive processes are used.

**Evaluation:** dialysis is effective enough to keep a person with kidney failure alive, but is less effective than kidneys: it runs only a few hours several times a week, so wastes and fluid build up between sessions, cannot actively regulate or make hormones, and can cause low blood pressure and infection.

questions.question: Eucalyptus trees typically live in dry habitats. Describe two adaptations of their leaves that help the tree conserve water.
questions.answer:
- Leaves hang vertically, presenting less surface to the midday sun, so they heat up less and lose less water.
- A thick waxy cuticle covers the leaf, reducing evaporation from the surface.

questions.question: Identify the cause and effect of a named nutritional disease you have studied.
questions.answer: **Scurvy** is caused by a dietary lack of vitamin C. Vitamin C is needed to form stable collagen, so deficiency causes swollen, bleeding gums, loose teeth, easy bruising and poor wound healing.

questions.question: The diagram shows a structure involved in protein synthesis. Explain the stage of protein synthesis that involves structure K.
questions.answer: Structure K is a **ribosome**, which carries out **translation**. It binds mRNA and starts at the start codon (AUG). Each codon is paired with the complementary anticodon of a tRNA carrying a specific amino acid. The ribosome joins adjacent amino acids with peptide bonds, moves along one codon, and releases the empty tRNA. This repeats until a stop codon is reached, when the polypeptide is released.

questions.question: The family tree includes individuals affected by a hereditary disorder. I-2 (individual 2) has the disorder; her husband I-1 does not. Is the disorder most likely autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive? Explain with reference to the family tree.
questions.answer: **Autosomal recessive.** Individuals 3 and 4 are unaffected but have an affected child (10). With a dominant allele an affected child needs an affected parent, so both 3 and 4 must be heterozygous carriers.

questions.question: The family tree includes individuals affected by a hereditary disorder. I-2 (individual 2) has the disorder; her husband I-1 does not. The disorder is autosomal recessive. What is the genotype of individual 4 (generation II)?
questions.answer: Heterozygous (Aa): she is unaffected but inherited a recessive allele from her affected mother.

questions.question: The graph shows changes in hormones in the blood after fertilisation. Explain why progesterone from the placenta was not produced until 5 weeks post fertilisation.
questions.answer: The placenta takes time to develop after implantation and cannot secrete progesterone until about week 5. Before then, progesterone needed to maintain the uterine lining is supplied by the corpus luteum.

questions.question: The graph shows changes in hormones in the blood after fertilisation. For ONE hormone other than placental progesterone, describe its function with specific reference to the graph.
questions.answer: **Oxytocin** stimulates contraction of the uterus during labour. The graph shows it is essentially absent until about 36–37 weeks, then rises sharply to a peak at about 39–40 weeks (birth), when strong contractions are needed, and falls away by about 42 weeks after delivery.

questions.question: With the aid of a specific example, assess the impact of artificial pollination on the composition and continuity of a population.
questions.answer:
Artificial pollination is the manual transfer of pollen from chosen plants to the stigmas of others (with the target flowers protected from other pollen). **Example:** wheat breeders crossing a high-yielding variety with a rust-resistant variety.

**Composition:** selected alleles (resistance, yield) increase in frequency. Initially the cross creates new combinations, but repeatedly using a few elite parents reduces genetic diversity and other alleles may be lost.

**Continuity:** well-chosen varieties survive and reproduce better under the targeted pressure (rust), supporting continuity. However, a genetically uniform crop is vulnerable to a new disease or environmental change.

**Assessment:** the impact is large: it is a powerful, fast way to improve a population, but long-term continuity depends on keeping diversity (e.g. seed banks and wild relatives).

questions.question: Compare and contrast chromosomal mutations and point mutations.
questions.answer:
- Similarity: both are permanent changes to DNA that can arise from mutagens or errors in cell division/replication, and are heritable if in germ cells.
- Scale: point mutations change a single base pair (or a few); chromosomal mutations change large segments or arrangement of chromosomes, affecting many genes.
- Mechanism and effect: point mutations arise mainly during DNA replication or from damage, often altering at most one protein; chromosomal mutations (deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation) arise from chromosome breakage or faulty crossing over and usually have larger effects.

questions.question: The dolphin *Delphinus delphis* has a diploid number of 44. In a mutation observed in a male dolphin, chromosome 9 became permanently attached to chromosome 18 (the centromere of 18 being lost in the fusion). The diagram shows chromosomes 9 and 18 in a normal male and in the male with the mutation. The male with the mutation has 43 chromosomes in each somatic cell but a normal phenotype. Explain why.
questions.answer: All the genetic information is still present: the genes of chromosomes 9 and 18 are simply joined on one chromosome (only a non-essential centromere region is lost). The normal proteins are made in normal amounts, so the phenotype is normal.

questions.answer:

questions.question: Genes can be cloned in various ways. One method is shown in the diagram. Identify and describe this process and how it can be used to clone a gene.
questions.answer: This is **recombinant DNA technology** using a plasmid. The plasmid and the foreign DNA are cut with the same restriction enzyme, producing complementary ends. DNA ligase joins them into a recombinant plasmid, which is put into a bacterium. As the bacterium divides (and the plasmid replicates), many copies of the inserted gene are made.

questions.question: Genes can be cloned in various ways. One method is shown in the diagram. Another method of gene cloning is the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Contrast PCR with the process in the diagram.
questions.answer:
- PCR copies DNA in a test tube (in vitro); plasmid cloning relies on living bacteria (in vivo).
- PCR uses primers, Taq polymerase and repeated temperature cycles; plasmid cloning uses restriction enzymes and ligase.
- PCR only copies a DNA sequence and takes hours; plasmid cloning creates a new recombinant combination, takes longer, and the bacteria can also express the gene.

questions.question: A species of tomato was genetically engineered to contain a gene making it resistant to some pests (a GM plant). Discuss the social, economic and cultural considerations surrounding GM plants, with reference to this tomato and another example of a GM plant.
questions.answer:
**Examples:** the pest-resistant tomato; Bt cotton (produces an insecticidal protein from *Bacillus thuringiensis*). Golden Rice (enriched in beta-carotene) is a further example.

**Social:** pest resistance can mean less pesticide exposure for farm workers and consumers; Golden Rice could reduce vitamin A deficiency. Concerns include possible allergens, uncertainty about long-term effects, demands for labelling and unequal access for poorer farmers.

**Economic:** higher, more reliable yields and lower spraying costs (seen with Bt cotton) raise farm income and could lower tomato prices. However, patented seed must often be bought each season with licence fees, concentrating control in a few companies; resistant pests may evolve; GM crops may be rejected by some export markets.

**Cultural:** some people object to "tampering with nature" or to transferring genes between species on religious or ethical grounds; traditional seed saving and local varieties, including those important to Indigenous communities, may be displaced or contaminated by gene flow.

**Judgement:** GM crops offer clear benefits, but acceptance depends on safety testing, resistance management, fair access and respect for consumer choice.

questions.question: Two patients with hearing loss see the same doctor: one is recommended a hearing aid and the other a cochlear implant. With reference to the structure and function of the ear, explain why different technologies are recommended.
questions.answer:
Sound passes the outer ear to the tympanic membrane, is amplified by the ossicles, and reaches the cochlea, where hair cells convert vibrations into nerve impulses carried by the auditory nerve.

A **hearing aid** has a microphone, amplifier and speaker: it makes sound louder in the ear canal. It suits mild to severe loss where the cochlea still has enough working hair cells (or reduced sound transmission can be overcome by amplification).

A **cochlear implant** has an external microphone, speech processor and transmitter, plus an implanted receiver and electrode array in the cochlea. It bypasses damaged hair cells and stimulates the auditory nerve directly. It suits severe to profound sensorineural loss, where amplification would not help.

The patients therefore have damage of different type or severity.

*Note: the school suggests implants treat profound conductive loss; they are used for sensorineural loss (conductive loss is treated by surgery or bone-conduction devices).*

questions.question: Cervical cancer usually develops between ages 20 and 50. Pap smears (detecting abnormal cervical cells) became widely used in Australia in the mid-1980s. In 2007 a vaccination program against human papillomavirus (HPV), associated with cervical cancer, began for girls aged 12–15. The graph shows the age-standardised incidence of cervical cancer in Australian women, 1982–2017. Explain the trend between 1982 and 2002.
questions.answer: Incidence fell from about 5.2 to about 2 per 100 000. Widespread Pap smear screening detected precancerous abnormalities, which could be treated before they became cancer.

questions.question:
Cervical cancer usually develops between ages 20 and 50. Pap smears (detecting abnormal cervical cells) became widely used in Australia in the mid-1980s. In 2007 a vaccination program against human papillomavirus (HPV), associated with cervical cancer, began for girls aged 12–15.

Describe each of the trends shown in the table.

- 20–24: rose to a peak of 21 in 2008, then decreased to 12.
- 25–29: little overall change, between 15 and 18.

questions.question:
Cervical cancer usually develops between ages 20 and 50. Pap smears (detecting abnormal cervical cells) became widely used in Australia in the mid-1980s. In 2007 a vaccination program against human papillomavirus (HPV), associated with cervical cancer, began for girls aged 12–15. The age-standardised incidence of cervical cancer fell from about 5.2 per 100 000 in 1982 to about 2 in 2002, then levelled off at about 1.6–2 to 2017.

Incidence per 1000 women screened, by age:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Year} & {<}20 & 20\text{–}24 & 25\text{–}29 & 30\text{–}34\\\hline 2005&10&17&15&9\\2006&11&16&15&9\\2007&10&18&16&10\\2008&12&21&17&12\\2009&8&18&18&11\\2010&6&17&17&12\\2011&5&15&18&13\\2012&6&15&18&13\\2013&5&14&17&14\\2014&4&12&15&14\\\hline\end{array}$$

Technologies such as genetic engineering are providing new avenues for disease prevention. Assess the effectiveness of these two technologies (Pap smears and the HPV vaccine) as prevention methods for cervical cancer, referring to the information and data.
questions.answer:
**The technologies.** Pap smears screen cells for abnormalities so they can be treated early. The HPV vaccine is a product of genetic engineering: the gene for the viral coat protein (L1) is inserted into yeast, which makes virus-like particles that contain no viral DNA. These stimulate antibodies and memory cells, preventing infection.

**Pap smears:** incidence fell from about 5.2 to 2 per 100 000 (1982–2002) as screening spread, showing high effectiveness. After about 2002 it plateaued near 1.6–2, so screening alone has limits: it depends on participation and test accuracy and does not prevent HPV infection.

**HPV vaccine:** from 2009 incidence in the table fell sharply for under-20s (12 to 4) and for 20–24-year-olds (21 to 12), the ages containing vaccinated girls. The 25–29 group changed little (few were vaccinated by 2014) and 30–34 rose (largely unvaccinated; may reflect better detection or behaviour). This is consistent with strong effectiveness, though the data are correlational.

**Limitations of the evidence:** longer follow-up of vaccinated cohorts is needed; the table is per 1000 screened women, far higher than the cancer rate, so it likely measures abnormalities rather than invasive cancer.

**Assessment:** both are effective and complementary. Screening reduces progression to cancer in all women who attend; vaccination prevents the main cause and is likely to reduce incidence further as vaccinated women age. Screening remains necessary because the vaccine does not cover every cancer-causing strain.

questions.question:
Pertussis is caused by the bacterium *Bordetella pertussis*. A vaccine is given to infants. The diagram shows the immune response to an infection.

Describe the role of plasma cells as shown in the diagram.
questions.answer: Plasma cells, formed from activated B cells, secrete large amounts of antibody specific to the *B. pertussis* antigen. Antibodies bind the antigen, forming antigen–antibody complexes that agglutinate and neutralise bacteria and mark them for destruction by phagocytes.

questions.question:
Pertussis is caused by the bacterium *Bordetella pertussis*. A vaccine is given to infants. The diagram shows the immune response to an infection.

Use the diagram and the graph to explain why a child vaccinated against pertussis will not get the disease.
questions.answer:
The vaccine is the initial exposure: it contains the antigen but does not cause disease. B cells with matching receptors are activated with help from helper T cells and form plasma cells and memory B cells. This primary response is slow and produces a relatively small antibody peak.

If the child later meets the bacterium (secondary exposure), memory cells recognise it and rapidly divide into plasma cells. The graph shows antibody production is faster, reaches a much higher concentration and lasts longer. The bacteria are destroyed before they multiply enough to cause symptoms.

questions.question:

questions.question: Gumbi Gumbi (*Pittosporum angustifolium*) is an Aboriginal bush medicine for coughs and colds, now sold to non-Indigenous people. Outline what 'bush medicine' means and explain why recognition and protection of Aboriginal cultural and intellectual property is important.
questions.answer:
Bush medicine is the traditional use by Aboriginal peoples of native plants and other natural materials to treat illness, based on knowledge passed down over many generations.

Protection matters because the knowledge belongs to the communities that developed it and is part of their culture. Without recognition, others can patent or commercialise it without consent. Protocols ensure free, informed consent, acknowledgement, a fair share of benefits that supports communities, and culturally appropriate, sustainable use of the plants.

questions.question:
The graphs show the incidence of skin melanoma and deaths by age for men and women (2009–2013).

Analyse and account for the trends shown.
questions.answer:
**Age:** new cases and deaths are essentially zero in childhood and rise with age, peaking at 80–84 years for new cases (about 165 per 100 000 men, 80 women); deaths are highest at 85+ (about 55 men, 22 women). UV damage to DNA accumulates over a lifetime, and mutations take time to build up in genes controlling cell division; immune surveillance and repair also decline with age.

**Sex:** from about 60 years, men have much higher rates than women (roughly double at the peak), and more deaths. Likely reasons include greater cumulative exposure through outdoor work, less use of sunscreen and protective clothing, and later diagnosis.

**Younger adults:** women have somewhat higher rates than men below about 50 years, possibly due to more deliberate tanning.

Deaths are far fewer than new cases, showing many melanomas are treated successfully.

questions.question:

questions.answer: Parents control children's sun protection and habits. UV exposure and sunburn in childhood add to lifetime DNA damage and raise melanoma risk later, so protecting children early gives the greatest benefit and establishes lifelong behaviour.

questions.question:

questions.question: Describe the cause, effects, treatment/management and means of prevention of a named nutritional disease OR disease caused by environmental exposure. Present the information in a table.
questions.answer:
**Asbestosis (environmental exposure)**

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| Cause | Inhaling asbestos fibres, which lodge in the lungs and cause chronic inflammation |
| Effects | Scarring (fibrosis) of lung tissue, reduced gas exchange, shortness of breath, cough; raised risk of lung cancer; can be fatal |
