5. Discovered that there were more wine-drinking respondents than spirits or beer-drinking respondents.
6. Removed some of the wine drinkers until both groups had equal numbers.
7. Analysed data, wrote the paper and published it in a scientific blog.

From the information provided, analyse the methodology used by this scientist.
questions.answer:
Strengths: a case-control design with a control group; matching by sex; a scientifically valid questionnaire.

Weaknesses:

- The sample (144 per group) is small, and the groups are only matched for sex; a larger, broader sample with other variables matched (age, ethnicity, etc.) and pair-matched controls would be better.
- Removing wine drinkers because of their responses introduces bias and reduces validity.
- The method looks at cirrhosis cases (incidence/prevalence), not mortality, so it cannot test the hypothesis about mortality rates.
- Self-reported questionnaire data may be inaccurate.
- Publishing in a blog means the work was not peer reviewed, so its reliability has not been checked.

Overall, the design cannot validly link spirits consumption to cirrhosis mortality.

questions.question: Which feature of DNA promotes easy replication?
questions.answer: Because each base pairs only with its complement (A with T, C with G), each strand of the double helix acts as a template for building a new complementary strand, so DNA can be copied accurately (A).
options: Complementary base pairing
Use of deoxyribose, not ribose
The sugar-phosphate backbone
The presence of nitrogen in the bases

questions.question: Which of the following processes increases the genetic variation between offspring of the same parents?
questions.answer: Crossing over in prophase I of meiosis exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, producing new allele combinations in the gametes and so more variation among offspring of the same parents (D). Mitosis and cloning produce identical cells; mutation is a rare random change rather than a regular source of variation between siblings.
options: Mitosis
Cloning
Mutation
Crossing over

questions.question: What is a behavioural adaptation in kangaroos that helps them cope with heat?
questions.answer: Resting (in shade) during the hottest part of the day is something the animal does, so it is a behavioural adaptation that reduces heat gain and heat production (A). The other options are not behaviours typical of kangaroos or are structural features.
options: They rest during the middle of the day.
They spend a lot of time wading in lakes.
They shelter in caverns to avoid direct sunlight.
Their feet and tail enable them to travel long distances very efficiently.

questions.question: There are four different nitrogenous bases in DNA. A sequence of fifty base pairs of nucleotides contains 17 adenine bases. How many cytosine bases are there in the sequence?
questions.answer: Fifty base pairs contain 100 bases. Adenine pairs with thymine, so there are 17 A and 17 T, i.e. 34 bases. The remaining 66 bases are G and C in equal numbers, so there are 33 cytosine (C).

questions.question: Three diseases are described. Mercury poisoning is caused by a build-up of ingested mercury in the body. Beriberi is caused by insufficient thiamine in the body. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is caused by an inability to make a particular functional enzyme. Which is the correct classification of these diseases as genetic, nutritional and environmental respectively?
questions.answer: G6PD deficiency is genetic (a faulty gene means the enzyme cannot be made), beriberi is nutritional (lack of thiamine in the diet) and mercury poisoning is environmental (exposure to a toxin) (C).
options: Mercury poisoning; beriberi; glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
Beriberi; mercury poisoning; mercury poisoning
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; beriberi; mercury poisoning
Mercury poisoning; glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; beriberi

questions.question: If a red-flowered snapdragon is crossed with a white-flowered one, all progeny are pink. When pink is crossed with pink, the progeny are in the ratio 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. What is the most correct prediction of the offspring ratio when a pink snapdragon is crossed with a white snapdragon?
questions.answer: This is incomplete dominance: red = $C^RC^R$, white = $C^WC^W$, pink = $C^RC^W$. Pink $\times$ white is $C^RC^W\times C^WC^W$, giving $\frac12C^RC^W$ (pink) and $\frac12C^WC^W$ (white), i.e. 1 pink : 1 white (A).
options: 1 pink : 1 white
1 pink : 3 white
1 pink : 2 white : 1 red
1 red : 2 pink : 1 white

questions.question:
After exposure to a virus responsible for influenza, the antibody levels of two individuals were measured over several days.

| Day | Individual A | Individual B |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 5 |
| 2 | 5 | 100 |
| 3 | 50 | 3500 |
| 4 | 1000 | 10000< |
| 5 | 10000< | 10000< |

Which individual(s) is more likely to have received the influenza vaccine?
questions.answer: Vaccination produces memory cells, so on exposure to the real virus there is a faster and larger secondary response. Individual B's antibody count rises much more rapidly (reaching 3500 by day 3 and its peak by day 4), consistent with prior vaccination (B).
options: Individual A, as their antibody counts increased more rapidly.
Individual B, as their antibody counts increased more rapidly.
Neither individual as their antibody levels both peak at 10000<.
Both individuals as their antibody level both peak at 10000.

questions.question: If the template strand of a DNA molecule has the sequence 3' CTTGGATCGA 5', which of the following mRNA strands would be produced?
questions.answer: mRNA is complementary to the template strand, with uracil replacing thymine, and runs antiparallel: template 3' C T T G G A T C G A 5' gives mRNA 5' G A A C C U A G C U 3' (D).
options: 5' CUUGGAUCGA 3'
5' GUUCCATCGA 3'
5' GAACCTAGCT 3'
5' GAACCUAGCU 3'

questions.question: A single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) is a DNA sequence variation in which a single nucleotide differs between members of a species. ACTN3 is a gene coding for the muscle protein alpha-actinin-3, with genotypes RR, RX and XX. Lack of the protein (XX) is not associated with disease. The chart shows the frequency of each genotype in different groups of athletes and in controls. What is the role of alpha-actinin-3?
questions.answer: The chart shows power athletes (especially power Olympians) almost never have the XX genotype, which is more common in controls and endurance athletes. People who make the protein (RR or RX) are over-represented among power athletes, so alpha-actinin-3 gives an advantage in becoming a power athlete (C).
options: Gives an advantage in becoming an endurance athlete.
Does not give an advantage in becoming an endurance athlete.
Gives an advantage in becoming a power athlete.
Does not give an advantage in becoming a power athlete.

questions.question: Choose the description that correctly identifies the characteristics of the genetic material in some types of infective agent. Match, in order: (i) contains no DNA or RNA – protein only; (ii) DNA or RNA in a protein coat; (iii) DNA in the cell cytoplasm; (iv) DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus.
questions.answer: Prions are infectious proteins with no nucleic acid; viruses have DNA or RNA inside a protein coat; bacteria are prokaryotes with DNA free in the cytoplasm; protozoa are eukaryotes with DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus (D).
options: (i) Virus; (ii) prion; (iii) bacterium; (iv) protozoan
(i) Prion; (ii) virus; (iii) protozoan; (iv) bacterium
(i) Virus; (ii) prion; (iii) protozoan; (iv) bacterium
(i) Prion; (ii) virus; (iii) bacterium; (iv) protozoan

questions.question: The picture shows a pair of homologous chromosomes in a cell at the beginning of anaphase I of meiosis. The reason this process results in increased variability of offspring in sexual reproduction is because
questions.answer: In anaphase I the homologous chromosomes separate, and the orientation of each pair on the equator is random and independent of other pairs (independent assortment). This produces many different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in the gametes, increasing variation (B).
options: Gametes produced have half the number of chromosomes.
This homologous pair moves independently of other pairs.
Sexual reproduction combines chromosomes from two individuals.
Mutations in homologous chromosomes occur readily at this stage.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct role of the lymph system in the immune response?
questions.answer: The lymph system (lymph nodes) houses lymphocytes, including the memory B and T cells that 'remember' pathogens previously encountered (D). Fever, apoptosis and barriers to entry are not roles of the lymphatic system.
options: Initiating a fever response.
Triggering cell death around the pathogen.
Preventing entry of pathogen into the body.
Holding a record of past invasion by pathogens.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of natural passive immunity to the measles virus?
questions.answer: Passive immunity is gained by receiving ready-made antibodies rather than making them. When this occurs naturally (via the placenta or breast milk) it is natural passive immunity (B). Injected antibodies are artificial passive immunity; weakened virus is artificial active; natural exposure is natural active.
options: Being injected with antibodies to the measles virus.
A baby receiving measles antibodies in breast milk.
Being injected with weakened strain of measles virus.
Being naturally exposed to the measles virus.

questions.question: Albinism is an inherited disorder characterised by the complete or partial absence of pigment in the skin, hair and eyes due to absence of an enzyme involved in the production of melanin. It affects both genders equally and can be found in the children of parents who do not show the disease. Which best describes the mechanism of inheritance for albinism?
questions.answer: Affected children born to unaffected parents means the parents are carriers of a hidden (recessive) allele. Both sexes are affected equally, so it is autosomal rather than sex-linked (A).
options: Recessive
Dominant
Sex-linked
Co-dominant

questions.question: In 2002 the first cloned cat (CC) was produced using a somatic cell from a calico cat (Rainbow). CC is not identical to Rainbow: Rainbow's coloured fur patches are not the same size and shape as those of her clone. What is the most probable explanation?
questions.answer: A clone made from a somatic cell has the same genotype as the donor, and meiosis (crossing over, independent assortment) is not involved. Differences in phenotype, such as the pattern of fur patches, arise from environmental influences (including conditions during development) on gene expression (B).
options: Crossing over during meiosis.
The influence of environment on phenotype.
Independent assortment of chromosomes in meiosis.
Expression of recessive genes from previous generations.

questions.question: In the search for a malaria vaccine, scientists have focused on circumsporozoite protein (CSP), which is secreted by the malaria parasite and present on its surface. For the vaccination to work, the scientists want CSP to act as
questions.answer: A vaccine works by presenting an antigen — a foreign molecule such as a surface protein — that triggers the adaptive immune response and memory cell production (A).
options: An antigen.
An allergen.
An antibody.
A complement protein.

questions.question: Consider the karyotype shown. The cell from which these chromosomes were taken
questions.answer: The karyotype is from a diploid human cell, so each numbered autosome is a homologous pair, one inherited from each parent (D). The diploid number is 46 (not 44), the presence of a Y chromosome shows a male, and chromosome 18 appears three times (trisomy 18), so it does not have two copies of chromosome 18 genes.
options: Has a diploid number of 44.
Comes from a human female.
Has two copies of each of the genes found on chromosome 18.
Has inherited one chromosome number 4 from the mother and inherited one chromosome number 4 from the father.

questions.question: Advances in DNA technology have made it possible to carry out genetic screening for particular genetic diseases. Some people may decide not to have children based on the result of their genetic screening. This decision will
questions.answer: If carriers or affected people choose not to reproduce, the harmful allele is passed on less often, so its frequency in the gene pool changes, which is evolution of the population (A). It does not alter the DNA itself, increase variation, or eliminate the allele completely (carriers can still carry it).
options: Alter the frequency of an allele and will, therefore, have an impact on future human evolution.
Have no impact on future human evolution since the genes or DNA are not altered in the testing.
Increase genetic variation in the human population and will, therefore, have an impact on future human evolution.
Result in complete loss of an allele from a population and will, therefore, have an impact on future human evolution.

questions.question: The diagram shows four pathogens (R, S, T, U) with different surface markers and three antibodies (E, F, G). Which one of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: An antibody is effective only against pathogens bearing the antigen whose shape matches its binding site. Antibody F's binding sites match antigens on three of the four pathogens (B).
options: Antibody E would be effective against both pathogen S and pathogen R.
Antibody F is effective against three of the pathogens.
There are no antibodies effective against pathogen U.
Antibody G is only effective against pathogen R.

questions.question: Four cuttings were made from a single hydrangea plant and grown into established plants (an ancient form of cloning), then planted in four separate locations in a backyard. Hydrangea flowers change colour according to the pH of the soil. Using your knowledge of genotypic and phenotypic expression, explain why these clones had different coloured flowers.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The cuttings are clones, so all four plants have the same genotype. However, phenotype is determined by the genotype together with the environment. The four plants are growing in soil of different pH in different parts of the garden, and soil pH affects the expression of the flower-colour genes/pigment, so the flowers show different colours even though the plants are genetically identical.

questions.question: Hydrangea cuttings taken from one plant are grown into genetically identical plants. One of the plants became infected with a disease and died. Hypothesise how this disease might affect the other plants.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The other plants are genetically identical to the plant that died, so they have the same susceptibility to the pathogen. I hypothesise that they would also become infected and die if exposed to the disease (because there is no genetic variation, none is likely to have resistance).

questions.question: Hydrangeas are produced commercially using cuttings, a common asexual (vegetative) propagation method. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this method of agricultural production.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Advantages: each cutting produces a plant with the same desirable features as the parent plant, such as flower shape and density, so the product is uniform and predictable. Plants from cuttings also mature faster than those grown from seed, so they can be sold sooner, and the method is cheap, quick and needs no pollination or sexual partner. Disadvantages: because all the plants are clones with no genetic variation, they are all susceptible to the same diseases and pests, so one outbreak (or a change in conditions such as drought) could wipe out the whole stock. In addition, although genetically identical, flower colour depends on soil pH, so the plants will not all look the same unless grown in the same soil conditions. Overall the method is efficient for a stable, controlled environment but risky for the long term because of the lack of genetic diversity.

questions.question: Colour blindness is a disorder caused by mutant genes in the red and green cones in cone cells. Use the pedigree to infer the inheritance pattern of colour blindness. Provide evidence from the pedigree to support your answer.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Colour blindness is inherited as an X-linked (sex-linked) recessive trait. It is sex-linked because only males (the shaded squares) are affected in the pedigree, and no affected females appear. It is recessive because it can skip a generation: it is present in every second generation, with unaffected parents (carrier mothers) having an affected son, so the allele is hidden in carriers.

questions.question: On the pedigree, identify all potential carriers of colour blindness (those who would be shaded half).
questions.answer: Sample answer: Because the allele is X-linked recessive, carriers are unaffected females who have an affected father or an affected son (they must carry one copy of the allele), and unaffected daughters of carrier mothers could also be carriers. Shading these females gives the six half-shaded circles shown in the answer diagram, all other females being unaffected non-carriers or not at risk.

questions.question: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive. A carrier female married a colour-blind male. Use a Punnett square to determine the likelihood of them having a colour-blind daughter. Include genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring as percentages.
questions.answer:
Sample answer: Let $X^c$ be the colour-blind allele and $X$ the normal allele. Mother (carrier) $X X^c$; father (colour-blind) $X^cY$.

| | $X^c$ | $Y$ |
|---|---|---|
| $X$ | $XX^c$ | $XY$ |
| $X^c$ | $X^cX^c$ | $X^cY$ |

Offspring: 25% $XX^c$ (carrier daughter), 25% $X^cX^c$ (colour-blind daughter), 25% $XY$ (normal son), 25% $X^cY$ (colour-blind son). There is a 25% chance that any child will be a colour-blind daughter.

questions.question: The red kangaroo is an endotherm that lies in the shade as a behavioural adaptation to assist in cooling down during the heat of the day. Explain how ONE structural and ONE physiological adaptation that the kangaroo may be exhibiting helps it to cool itself.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Structural adaptation: the kangaroo's tall, thin ears have a large surface area and a network of blood capillaries close to the surface, so blood passing through them loses heat to the air and cools before returning to the body. Physiological adaptation: vasodilation — blood vessels under the skin widen so more warm blood flows near the skin surface, where heat is lost by radiation and by evaporation of sweat/saliva, lowering body temperature.

questions.question: The internal and external environments of organisms are constantly changing, and organisms have evolved systems to maintain homeostasis. Construct a diagram of a negative feedback loop to show how the human body regulates temperature when there is a change to its internal environment.
questions.answer: Sample answer (draw as a labelled loop): Stimulus: body temperature rises above the set point (or falls below it) → Receptors: thermoreceptors (skin and hypothalamus) detect the change → Control centre: the hypothalamus processes the information → Effectors: sweat glands, blood vessels in the skin (vasodilation), muscles/hair-erector cells → Response: sweating and vasodilation to lose heat (when too hot) or shivering, vasoconstriction and increased metabolic rate to gain/retain heat (when too cold) → body temperature returns to normal, which reduces the stimulus (negative feedback). The two directions of the loop are shown in the school's sample diagram.

questions.question: The graph shows blood glucose concentration of a healthy adult from morning to afternoon. The grey boxes represent the times during which hormones are released from the pancreas into the blood. What are the hormones represented by the boxes labelled A and B?
questions.answer: Sample answer: Box A (released when blood glucose is high, after eating) is insulin; box B (released when blood glucose has fallen) is glucagon.

questions.question: On a graph of blood glucose concentration over a day, an arrow at approximately 12.30 pm marks a change shortly before the glucose level rises. Suggest what event occurred at approximately 12.30 pm.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The person ate a meal (lunch), so glucose was absorbed into the blood and blood glucose began to rise.

prev.question: The graph shows blood glucose concentration of a healthy adult from morning to afternoon. The grey boxes represent the times during which hormones are released from the pancreas into the blood. What are the hormones represented by the boxes labelled A and B?
prev.answer: Sample answer: Box A (released when blood glucose is high, after eating) is insulin; box B (released when blood glucose has fallen) is glucagon.

questions.question: On the graph of blood glucose concentration, a dotted line is drawn at a blood glucose concentration of about 90 mg/100 cm³. Explain the significance of the dotted line.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The dotted line is the set point (normal level) of blood glucose that the body keeps within a narrow range around by negative feedback. When glucose rises above it, insulin is released to lower it; when it falls below it, glucagon is released to raise it. This keeps the internal environment stable, which is homeostasis.

prev.question: The graph shows blood glucose concentration of a healthy adult from morning to afternoon. The grey boxes represent the times during which hormones are released from the pancreas into the blood. What are the hormones represented by the boxes labelled A and B?
prev.answer: Sample answer: Box A (released when blood glucose is high, after eating) is insulin; box B (released when blood glucose has fallen) is glucagon.

prev.question: On a graph of blood glucose concentration over a day, an arrow at approximately 12.30 pm marks a change shortly before the glucose level rises. Suggest what event occurred at approximately 12.30 pm.
prev.answer: Sample answer: The person ate a meal (lunch), so glucose was absorbed into the blood and blood glucose began to rise.

questions.question: Indigenous bush foods have become a more significant part of Australian cuisine for their flavours and for their nutritional and medicinal properties. Identify a bush food you have studied and describe its Aboriginal and contemporary applications.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Kakadu plum is a small fruit that contains substantially more vitamin C than an orange. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have used it as a food to boost the body's nutrient levels and to combat or prevent illnesses such as scurvy. Its contemporary applications include its use as a natural vitamin C source in modern medicines and supplements, and in skin-care products for its antioxidant properties, which help restore skin elasticity.

questions.question: The graph plots the percentage of the population that is obese against income inequality for a range of countries. Describe the trend seen in the graph.
questions.answer: Sample answer: There is a positive correlation: as income inequality increases, so does the percentage of the population that is obese. Countries with low income inequality, such as Japan, Sweden and Norway, have a low obesity percentage (below about 12%), whereas countries with high income inequality, such as the USA and the UK, have a high obesity percentage (about 22–30%).

questions.question: The graph plots the percentage of the population that is obese against income inequality for a range of countries. Identify the approximate prevalence of obesity in Australia.
questions.answer: Sample answer: About 17–19%.

questions.question: The World Health Organisation declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020. In that month Australia implemented a hotel quarantine program requiring all returning travellers to undertake 14 days of quarantine. The United Kingdom implemented a similar program much later, in February 2021. Up to March 2021 Australia had 29 000 cases of COVID-19, while the UK had over 4.21 million. Select TWO disease preventive procedures from the following list and evaluate how these procedures can work together to minimise and control the COVID-19 pandemic: quarantine; hygiene practices; public health campaigns; vaccination.
questions.answer: Sample answer (quarantine and vaccination): Quarantine, as in Australia's hotel quarantine, isolates people who may be infected for the incubation period, preventing the virus from entering and spreading in the community. It was very effective: Australia had about 29 000 cases compared with over 4.2 million in the UK, which introduced quarantine about 11 months later. Its limitations are that it is costly, restricts freedom and travel, and any breach can seed an outbreak, so it can only delay and suppress the disease rather than provide lasting protection. Vaccination works by exposing the immune system to an antigen without causing the disease, so that memory cells are produced and the person can respond quickly if later infected. This protects individuals, reduces severity and transmission, and when a large proportion of the population is vaccinated, herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated. However, vaccines take time to develop, produce and distribute, may not be 100% effective, and depend on public uptake. The two procedures work together: quarantine buys time and keeps case numbers low while vaccines are developed and rolled out, preventing the health system being overwhelmed. Once most people are vaccinated, quarantine and border restrictions can be relaxed safely because the population is protected by immunity. Judgement: used together, quarantine and vaccination are more effective than either alone — quarantine gives the short-term control (as seen in Australia's much lower case numbers) and vaccination provides the long-term protection that allows the pandemic to be controlled, with hygiene practices and public health campaigns supporting both.

questions.question: What is the difference between meiosis and mitosis?
questions.answer: Sample answer: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells (46 chromosomes in humans), used for growth and repair of body (somatic) cells. Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells (23 chromosomes in humans), the gametes needed for sexual reproduction.

questions.question: How does cell replication contribute to the survival of a species?
questions.answer: Sample answer: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells (clones), so favourable characteristics are passed on unchanged, such as in plants that spread by runners. In multicellular organisms it provides the growth and repair of cells that allow individuals to survive and reproduce. Meiosis produces gametes with new combinations of alleles, through crossing over in prophase I, independent assortment and random fertilisation, which increases genetic variation in the population. A varied population is less likely to be wiped out by a sudden environmental change, so the species continues. Mutations that occur during either process can also create new alleles; those that are favourable may increase survival of the species, while harmful ones are lost through natural selection.

questions.question: A mysterious disease outbreak occurs in a colony of koalas around the Lucas Heights nuclear reactor. Ten sick animals have the same symptoms: weight loss, skin lesions and foul breath. Radioactive contamination is suspected, but blood tests show a type of bacterium in their blood. Describe the steps you would take to prove that this bacterium is the cause of the disease.
questions.answer: Sample answer (Koch's postulates): (1) Show that the bacterium is present in all of the sick animals (and absent from healthy koalas). (2) Isolate the bacterium from a sick animal and grow it in pure culture. (3) Inject the pure culture into a healthy koala and observe whether it develops the same symptoms. (4) Re-isolate the bacterium from the newly infected koala and culture it, and confirm that it is the same bacterium as in step 1. If all steps are met, the bacterium is the cause of the disease.

questions.question:
Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium. Data were recorded for the declining effectiveness of two drugs used to treat or prevent malaria.

| Year | Mefloquinone effectiveness (%) | Quinine effectiveness (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 1976 | 100 | 90 |
| 1978 | 100 | 85 |
| 1980 | 100 | 80 |
| 1984 | 100 | 72 |
| 1988 | 90 | 64 |
| 1990 | 70 | 58 |

Graph the data to compare the effectiveness of the two drugs over time.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Draw a line graph with year on the x-axis (an even scale, e.g. 1976–1990 in 2-year steps) and effectiveness (%) on the y-axis (using most of the axis, e.g. 50–100), with both lines labelled or in a key. Mefloquinone stays at 100% until 1984 then falls to 70% by 1990. Quinine falls steadily from 90% to 58%.

questions.question: Data show the effectiveness of two antimalarial drugs declining between 1976 and 1990: quinine fell from 90% to 58% and mefloquinone stayed at 100% until 1984 and then fell to 70% by 1990. Use the data to explain the impact of human processes on genetic diversity.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Human use of antimalarial drugs acts as a selection pressure on the Plasmodium population. Within the population there is genetic variation, and some individuals have alleles (from mutation) that make them resistant. When the drug is used, non-resistant parasites are killed, but resistant ones survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance alleles, so the proportion of resistant Plasmodium increases (natural selection). This is shown by the falling effectiveness of quinine from 90% to 58% over 14 years, and of mefloquinone from 1988 (100% to 70%). The gene pool of the parasite has been changed by human activity, favouring drug-resistant alleles and reducing the diversity of the non-resistant alleles.

questions.question: The advertisement shown ('Don't waste antibiotics on colds or flu', 'Antibiotics are losing their power', 'Join the fight against antibiotic resistance') was on a bus stop outside a school and was produced by a not-for-profit company funded by the Australian government. Explain the purpose of this advertising campaign.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The purpose is to educate the public that antibiotics only kill bacteria and are not effective against viruses such as those that cause colds and flu, so taking them for these illnesses is a waste. Overuse and misuse of antibiotics acts as a selection pressure that allows resistant bacteria to survive and multiply, so antibiotics are 'losing their power'. By changing people's behaviour (not asking for or using antibiotics unnecessarily and completing prescribed courses), the campaign aims to slow the spread of antibiotic resistance, protecting the effectiveness of these drugs.

questions.question: A child's mother has blood type A− and her father has blood type AB+. Identify which phenotypes are NOT possible for the child.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The mother is $I^AI^A$ or $I^Ai$ and rr; the father is $I^AI^B$ and RR or Rr. The child can receive $I^A$ or $I^B$ from the father and $I^A$ or $i$ from the mother, giving A, AB, or B (if the mother is $I^Ai$), and either Rh+ or Rh−. The child cannot be blood group O (it would need $ii$, but the father has no $i$ allele), so O+ and O− are not possible. (The school's answer lists only A and AB as possible; B is also possible if the mother is heterozygous $I^Ai$.)

questions.question: Describe TWO differences in inheritance patterns of the ABO blood group system and the Rhesus blood group system.
questions.answer: Sample answer: (1) The ABO system has three alleles ($I^A$, $I^B$, $i$), so it shows multiple alleles, whereas the Rhesus system has two alleles (R and r). (2) In the ABO system $I^A$ and $I^B$ are codominant (genotype $I^AI^B$ gives blood group AB, with both expressed) and both are dominant over $i$, whereas in the Rhesus system the R allele is completely dominant over r (RR and Rr are Rh+, only rr is Rh−). (The genes are also on different chromosomes, so they are inherited independently.)

questions.question: The diagram shows the DNA fingerprints of two parents (2 and 3), their two biological children and their adopted child. Which of individuals 1, 4 or 5 is the adopted child? Justify with reference to the picture.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Individual 5 is the adopted child. Each band in a biological child's DNA profile must be present in at least one parent. Individuals 1 and 4 have bands that match bands in parent 2 or parent 3, but individual 5 has several bands that do not match either parent.

questions.question: Explain why DNA fingerprinting uses sections of repeating sets of bases, rather than functional genes, for identification.
questions.answer: Sample answer: DNA fingerprinting uses short tandem repeats in non-coding DNA. The number of repeats at each site varies greatly between unrelated individuals, so the pattern of fragment lengths is highly specific to an individual (except identical twins) and can be used to identify them or establish relatedness. Functional genes code for proteins that are essential for life, so they are very similar between individuals (variation is limited because most changes would be harmful), and therefore cannot discriminate between individuals.

questions.question: The graph shows changes in female hormone levels in blood during the forty weeks of pregnancy (progesterone rising from about week 4, oestrogen rising from about week 20, oxytocin spiking around week 40). Explain why progesterone levels in the blood increase dramatically from week 4 of pregnancy.
questions.answer: Sample answer: After implantation, the placenta develops and begins to produce progesterone (in addition to the corpus luteum early on). The placenta's production increases as it grows, so blood progesterone rises steadily. Progesterone maintains the uterine lining and prevents contractions, which keeps the pregnancy going.

questions.question: The graph shows female hormone levels in blood during the forty weeks of pregnancy. For ONE hormone other than progesterone, describe its function with specific reference to the graph.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Oxytocin: its level is very low until about week 39–40, when it increases sharply to a peak around week 40, and falls again after birth. Oxytocin stimulates strong contractions of the uterine muscle, which cause labour and the birth of the baby; the contractions stimulate further oxytocin release (positive feedback), explaining the sharp spike at the end of pregnancy. (Alternatively, oestrogen: low until week 20, then rising to a peak around week 38 before birth, it stimulates growth of the uterus and mammary glands, and in late pregnancy increases the sensitivity of the uterus to oxytocin.)

questions.question: What is the best definition of a *mutagen*?
questions.answer: A mutagen is an agent (for example UV radiation, X-rays or certain chemicals) that causes mutation, that is, genetic change (B). A is the definition of a mutation.
options: A change in the structure of DNA.
An agent that causes genetic change.
The action or process of nucleotide change.
The rearrangement of sections of chromosomes and genes.

questions.question: Which of the following cell types initiates the secondary immune response depicted below?
questions.answer: On second exposure to the same antigen, memory B cells formed during the primary response recognise it and rapidly divide into plasma cells, giving a faster, larger antibody response (B).
options: cytotoxic T cell
memory B cell
helper T cell
suppressor T cell

questions.question:
Four ways of being immune are:

1. having memory cells after an infection
2. having memory cells after being injected with dead bacteria
3. being injected with antibodies
4. receiving antibodies from breast milk

Which row in the table correctly shows the types of immunity?

| | natural active | artificial active | natural passive | artificial passive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| B | 1 | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| C | 2 | 1 | 3 | 4 |
| D | 2 | 1 | 4 | 3 |
questions.answer: Active immunity means the body makes its own memory cells: after an infection it is natural (1), after a vaccine (dead bacteria) it is artificial (2). Passive immunity means antibodies are received: from breast milk it is natural (4), by injection it is artificial (3). So the row is 1, 2, 4, 3 (B).
options: A
B
C
D

questions.question: A pathogen was found to be prokaryotic, contain DNA and have a cell wall. How would it be classified?
questions.answer: Prokaryotic cells with DNA and a cell wall are bacteria. Viruses are not cellular, and fungi and protozoa are eukaryotic (D).
options: Virus
Fungus
Protozoan
Bacterium

questions.question: Skin grafting involves the transplantation of healthy skin which can be used to cover damaged skin, for example due to burns. A graft of skin tissue received from a different person is usually rejected by the recipient's body. Which statement about graft rejection is correct?
questions.answer: The paper's key is D: the recipient's immune system recognises the donor cells' surface antigens as foreign, and B-lymphocytes produce antibodies that react with them. (Note: T-cell-mediated rejection, as in B, is also a recognised mechanism; C is wrong because T-lymphocytes do not make antibodies.)
options: The graft is rejected by B-lymphocytes because T-lymphocytes are not stimulated to produce antibodies.
The graft is rejected by T-lymphocytes because they circulate in the blood and can gather at the graft site.
The graft is rejected by T-lymphocytes because the graft tissue causes T-lymphocytes to release antibodies.
The graft is rejected by B-lymphocytes because they make and release antibodies which react with the surface antigens on the graft cells.

questions.question:
The diagram below shows one way of testing the effect of an antibiotic on bacteria. The table shows the results of testing five different types of bacteria using the method above. Zones of less than 13 mm show the presence of resistant bacteria.

| Type of bacteria | Diameter of zone with no bacterial growth after 5 days (mm) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 14.30 |
| 2 | 0.00 |
| 3 | 10.90 |
| 4 | 0.00 |
| 5 | 20.40 |

Which statement can be supported by this data?
questions.answer: Zones under 13 mm indicate resistance. Types 2 (0.00 mm), 3 (10.90 mm) and 4 (0.00 mm) are below 13 mm, so only these are resistant (D). Type 3 is not treatable, so A is wrong; the data cannot show what happens over time (B, C).
options: The antibiotic can be used to treat bacteria types 1 and 3 only.
All the types of bacteria become resistant to antibiotics over time.
Type 5 of the bacteria can never become resistant to the antibiotic.
Only types 2, 3 and 4 of the bacteria show resistance to the antibiotic.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a function of a macrophage?
questions.answer: Macrophages are phagocytes found in tissues; they engulf pathogens and secrete cytokines that signal other immune cells (B). Histamine is released by mast cells and basophils, antigens are not produced by macrophages, and cytotoxins are released by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells.
options: They release histamines.
They are found in tissues and secrete cytokines in response to infection.
They circulate in the blood and produce antigens in response to infection.
They can leave the blood and secrete cytotoxins when exposed to damaged cells.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the benefit(s) of artificial insemination of dairy cattle?
questions.answer: Semen from one high-quality bull can be collected, diluted and used to inseminate many cows on many farms, spreading desirable milk-production traits (C). The offspring are not clones (A) or genetically modified (D).
options: The process creates genetically identical offspring that all produce good milk yield.
It decreases genetic diversity by introducing the same genes to different populations on different farms.
It enables a large number of cows to be inseminated with sperm from a bull with desirable milk production traits.
The process creates genetically modified calves that may produce milk in the future that is safe for human consumption.

questions.question:
Which row is the best comparison of the daughter cell produced in each process?

| | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| A | Identical to parent; identical to each other; homologous pairs of chromosomes | Different to parent; different to each other; unpaired chromosomes |
| B | Different to parent; identical to each other; homologous pairs of chromosomes | Identical to parent; different to each other; unpaired chromosomes |
| C | Identical to parent; different to each other; unpaired chromosomes | Different to parent; identical to each other; homologous pairs of chromosomes |
| D | Identical to parent; identical to each other; unpaired chromosomes | Different to parent; different to each other; homologous pairs of chromosomes |
questions.answer: Mitosis produces diploid daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell and to each other, with homologous pairs. Meiosis produces haploid gametes that differ from the parent and from each other (crossing over, independent assortment) and have unpaired chromosomes (A).
options: A
B
C
D

questions.question: Which statement best describes how cloning might be used to assist human health?
questions.answer: Therapeutic cloning could produce tissues and organs genetically matched to a patient to replace diseased or damaged ones (C). A clone is a separate organism, so A is wrong.
options: Human clones will mean an individual can 'live' forever.
Antibiotic resistant bacteria can be used to produce medicines.
Human organs could be cloned to replace diseased or damaged organs.
Food from cloned plants and animals can be modified to be healthier for human consumption.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a physiological adaptation in an endotherm that assists in maintaining homeostasis?
questions.answer: Physiological adaptations are internal functions. Vasoconstriction of surface blood vessels reduces heat loss in a cold environment (C). A is structural and B and D are behavioural (D is also an ectotherm).
options: Animals in cold climates having thick fur coats.
A dog moving into the shade to keep cool on a hot day.
Surface blood vessels in a human constricting on a cold day.
Lizards moving into the sunlight to raise their body temperature.

questions.question: The diagram models the process of fertilisation (sperm cells surrounding an egg cell). Which of the following is an appropriate evaluation of this model?
questions.answer: An evaluation of a model judges its strengths and limitations. D identifies a strength (simplicity) and a limitation (inaccurate relative sizes). A is only a description, B is only negative, and C wrongly claims reliability (a single sperm enters the egg, so not all stages are shown) (D).
options: The diagram shows the entry of sperm cells into the egg.
The diagram has some downfalls, such as the egg is too large.
The diagram is a very reliable model of fertilisation because it shows all the stages of fertilisation.
The diagram is good because it depicts fertilisation in a simple way, despite inaccuracies such as the size of cells.

questions.question: Grapefruit originated from a cross between an orange and a pomelo. What is this an example of?
questions.answer: Crossing two varieties/species to combine desirable traits is selective breeding (C). Transgenics involves inserting genes from another species.
options: Cloning
Transgenics
Selective breeding
Artificial insemination

questions.question: A chemical mutagen is known to cause significant damage to DNA structure through the disruption of the normal base-pairing process. A graph shows a positive linear relationship between mutagen vapour concentration (ppm) on the horizontal axis and the number of base-pairing errors on the vertical axis. Which of the following statements correctly describes the trend observed?
questions.answer: The independent variable (mutagen vapour concentration) is on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable (base-pairing errors) increases with it, so more mutagen leads to more errors (C).
options: An increased frequency of base-pairing errors leads to increased mutations.
An increased number of base-pairing errors leads to increased vapour production.
An increase in mutagen vapour concentration leads to an increase in the frequency of base-pairing errors.
An increase in mutagen vapour concentration leads to a decrease in the frequency of base-pairing errors.

questions.question: Some organisms have genotypes that produce three different phenotypes, for example a red flower crossed with a white flower to produce a pink flower. If two of these pink flowers were crossed, which of the following graphs would correctly represent the offspring of this cross?
questions.answer: This is incomplete dominance: pink flowers are heterozygous (RW). RW × RW gives 1 RR (red) : 2 RW (pink) : 1 WW (white), i.e. 25% : 50% : 25%, which is graph C (three bars with the middle one twice as tall).
options: Graph A
Graph B
Graph C
Graph D

questions.question: The graph shows the changes of three hormones during gestation (pregnancy). Which of the statements below best identifies the changes in hormone levels shown over the gestation period?
questions.answer: The curve peaking at about 8 weeks and then falling is hCG. The two other curves (oestrogen and progesterone) rise steadily through gestation and fall sharply at birth (about 40 weeks) (C).
options: hCG and oestrogen both rise and stay high in concentration from 24 weeks onwards.
Progesterone levels peak at 8 weeks then drop when the placenta is formed.
Both oestrogen and progesterone gradually rise in concentration until birth where they both rapidly decline at around 40 weeks.
hCG, produced by cells surrounding the embryo and then the placenta, peaks at around week 36 and can be detected in urine tests.

questions.question: Analyse the diagram which shows two pairs of homologous chromosomes and their allele arrangement. Assuming there is no crossing over, which of the following shows all the possible genotypes for the gametes formed in this organism?
questions.answer: Without crossing over, alleles on the same chromosome stay together. Pair 1 chromosomes are A B c and A b C; pair 2 chromosomes are D e and d E. Independent assortment gives 2 × 2 = 4 gametes: ABc+De, ABc+dE, AbC+De, AbC+dE, i.e. ABcDe, ABcdE, AbCDe, AbCdE (A).
options: ABcDe, ABcdE, AbCDe, AbCdE
AbCdE, ABCdE, AbCDE, AbCdE
ABcDE, ABcdE, AbCDe, AbDdE
AbcDE, ABcdE, AbCDe, ABcdE

questions.question: Which of the following represents the DNA sequence that codes for the mRNA strand shown below? mRNA: 5'–CUAACG–3'
questions.answer: The DNA template strand is complementary to the mRNA and antiparallel: mRNA 5'-C U A A C G-3' pairs with 3'-G A T T G C-5'. DNA contains thymine, not uracil, so B and C are wrong (A).
options: 3'–GATTGC–5'
3'–GAUUGC–5'
3'–CGUUAG–5'
3'–CGTTAG–5'

questions.question: Analyse the graph which shows blood glucose regulation (the effects of insulin and glucagon on blood sugar levels). Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: H is where blood glucose has fallen below its set point, so glucagon is released to raise it; this is where glucagon is highest (B). Insulin peaks when blood glucose is highest, not at A, and the set point is about 90 mg/100 mL, not 140.
options: Insulin is highest at A.
Glucagon is highest at H.
Insulin levels are high whenever the blood glucose levels reach 90 mg/mL.
According to this graph the optimal blood glucose concentration is 140 mg/100 mL.

questions.question: There were 15 cases of thyroid cancer recorded in Iceland between December 2009 and January 2011. The graph shows, for each case, the month of diagnosis (▲) and month of recovery (▼) or death (X) from the disease. Iceland has a population of 330 000 people. Which of the options below was the incidence rate (per 100 000) of thyroid cancer from March to October 2010?
questions.answer: Incidence counts new cases (diagnoses ▲) in the period: six cases were diagnosed between March and October 2010. Incidence rate $=\dfrac{6}{330\,000}\times100\,000\approx1.8$ per 100 000 (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows a stage of polypeptide synthesis. Identify the stage of polypeptide synthesis in this diagram.
questions.answer: Translation.

questions.question: The diagram shows translation at a ribosome, in which tRNA molecules with anti-codons bring amino acids to the mRNA. Why is the anti-codon significant in this process?
questions.answer: The anti-codon is a triplet of bases on a tRNA molecule that is complementary to a codon on the mRNA. This means that the tRNA, with its attached amino acid, binds to the correct codon, so amino acids are joined in the correct order to form a functional polypeptide (protein).

questions.question: The diagram shows the process of cross-pollination in plants, similar to the method Mendel used in his experiments (pollen transferred with a brush from one flower to the stigma of another flower whose anthers have been removed). Which step ensures the validity of the cross-pollination? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: Removal of the anthers. This prevents self-pollination, ensuring that only the transferred pollen fertilises the ova, so the parents of the offspring are known and the results of the cross are valid.

questions.question: The pea plant species in the diagram has two phenotypes for pea colour, green and yellow. Both parent plants are homozygous, and the plant providing the pollen produces yellow peas. Only green peas were produced (see diagram). Identify the dominant and recessive phenotypes for pea colour in this species.
questions.answer: Dominant: green. Recessive: yellow. (Crossing two homozygous parents gave only green offspring, so green is dominant.)

questions.question: In the cross-pollination in the diagram, both parent plants are homozygous and only green peas were produced. Determine the phenotype and genotype ratios of the offspring produced when crossing two plants grown from the peas in this diagram.
questions.answer:
Let G = green (dominant) and g = yellow (recessive). The parents of the diagram were GG and gg, so the peas produced (and the plants grown from them) are all heterozygous, Gg. Cross Gg × Gg:

| | G | g |
|---|---|---|
| **G** | GG | Gg |
| **g** | Gg | gg |

Genotype ratio: 1 GG : 2 Gg : 1 gg. Phenotype ratio: 3 green : 1 yellow. (Note that the genotype ratio is different from the phenotype ratio, because GG and Gg are both green.)

questions.question: The diagram shows the gene pool of a population over 20 generations (R and r alleles). Describe how the population has changed over the 20 generations.
questions.answer: In generation 1 both alleles are common and the population contains RR, Rr and rr individuals (the R and r alleles are about equally frequent). By generation 10 the R allele has become much less frequent, and by generation 20 the R allele has disappeared from the gene pool, leaving only the r allele (all individuals are rr).

questions.question: The diagram shows the gene pool of a population over 20 generations, in which the R allele declines and is lost. Explain how the changes in the gene pool may have occurred.
questions.answer: Natural selection may have acted on the population. If the R allele produces a trait that is not favourable in this environment, individuals with that trait are less likely to survive and reproduce, so they pass on fewer R alleles. Individuals with the rr genotype are better suited, survive and pass on r alleles. Over 20 generations the frequency of R decreased until it was removed from the gene pool. (Genetic drift in a small population could also cause an allele to be lost by chance.)

questions.question: The diagram shows the gene pool of a population in generation 10, which contains 32 alleles (8 are R and 24 are r). Calculate the allele frequency for the two alleles present in generation 10.
questions.answer: Frequency of R $=\dfrac{8}{32}=0.25$ (25%). Frequency of r $=\dfrac{24}{32}=0.75$ (75%), which is also $1-0.25$.

questions.question: Analyse the pedigree below showing a genetic condition expressed in a family. Determine the pattern of inheritance shown in this pedigree and identify the genotypes of individuals 1 and 16. Use the letter 'A' or 'a' to represent alleles.
questions.answer: Pattern of inheritance: autosomal recessive. Individuals 8 and 9 are both unaffected but have an affected child (17), so the condition is recessive, and an affected daughter (17) of an unaffected father (9) shows it is not X-linked. Individual 1 is affected: genotype aa. Individual 16 is unaffected, and both parents (8 and 9) must be carriers (Aa), so 16 is either AA or Aa.

questions.question: Analyse the pedigree. The condition is autosomal recessive, and individual 16 is unaffected with a genotype of AA or Aa. If individual 16 has a child with an affected partner (who has the genetic condition), what are the chances this child will be affected? Show any relevant working.
questions.answer:
The affected partner is aa. If 16 is Aa: Aa × aa gives Aa, aa, Aa, aa, so 2 in 4 (50%) of the children would be affected. If 16 is AA: AA × aa gives all Aa, so 0% would be affected.

| | A | a |
|---|---|---|
| **a** | Aa | aa |
| **a** | Aa | aa |

| | A | A |
|---|---|---|
| **a** | Aa | Aa |
| **a** | Aa | Aa |

Since 16's parents are both Aa, 16 is AA with probability 1/3 and Aa with probability 2/3, so the overall chance of an affected child is $\frac23\times\frac12=\frac13$ (about 33%). (Note: the school's example states '2 in 8 (25%)' for the Aa × aa cross, which is incorrect; the correct chance for that cross is 2 in 4, or 50%.)

questions.question: The diagram shows the result of crossing over during meiosis (a pair of replicated homologous chromosomes with alleles A/a, B/b and D/d). Identify the genotype of the parent cell.
questions.answer: Aa Bb Dd (the parent cell is heterozygous for all three genes).

questions.question: The diagram shows the neurons and parts of the body involved in a response to touching a hot object. Outline the stimulus–response pathway for this scenario by identifying the receptor, the effector and the response.
questions.answer: Stimulus: hot object. Receptor: thermoreceptors (pain/temperature receptors) in the skin. The sensory neuron carries the impulse to the CNS (spinal cord), where it is passed to a motor neuron. The motor neuron carries the impulse to the effector: the muscle cells in the arm. Response: the arm moves away from the hot object.

questions.question: DNA has both coding and non-coding segments, which vary in terms of biological function. The difference in function also means that the location of genetic mutations can change the impact on the function of the cell. Complete a table to distinguish between coding and non-coding DNA in terms of (i) biological function and (ii) an example of how biological function can be impacted by a mutation.
questions.answer:
| | Coding DNA | Non-coding DNA |
|---|---|---|
| Biological function | Codes for proteins (genes): transcribed to mRNA and translated into polypeptides, e.g. enzymes and structural proteins. | Does not code for proteins, but has other roles: regulation of gene expression (turning genes on and off), structural support for chromosomes (centromeres, telomeres), and coding for functional RNAs such as rRNA and tRNA. |
| Impact of a mutation | A point mutation (e.g. substitution causing a premature stop codon or a frameshift from an insertion or deletion) can change the amino acid sequence, producing a non-functional or altered protein and possibly disease. | A mutation in a regulatory region can turn genes on or off at the wrong time; a mutation in the centromere or telomere can cause chromosomes to be unable to separate correctly (non-disjunction) or to be damaged during replication, leading to aneuploidy or disease such as cancer. |

questions.question: Prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in Australian men. Prostate Specific Antigen (PSA) is a protein secreted within the prostate gland. The normal function of this protein is as a component of semen. It is coded for by the *KLK3* gene on chromosome 19. PSA is normally very high in men who are developing prostate cancer. Using a flow diagram (or ordered steps), describe how the *KLK3* gene produces PSA.
questions.answer:
1. The KLK3 gene (in the nucleus) is transcribed: RNA polymerase makes KLK3 mRNA complementary to the DNA template.
2. The mRNA leaves the nucleus and moves into the cytoplasm, where it attaches to a ribosome.
3. Translation: tRNA molecules bring the corresponding amino acids to the codons on the mRNA.
4. The amino acids are joined into a polypeptide, which folds into the PSA protein.

questions.question: In a recent article it was stated that 11.8% of men who have metastatic (spreading) prostate cancer also have germ-line mutations in certain repair genes (Prichard et al, 2016). This is significantly more than in the general male population. What is meant by germ-line mutations?
questions.answer: A mutation occurring in a germ cell (cell that will become a gamete), which can then be inherited by offspring.

questions.question: Explain why the effect of germ-line mutations on organisms is more severe than somatic mutations.
questions.answer: A germ-line mutation is present in the gamete, so it can be passed on to offspring. The zygote carrying the mutation undergoes mitosis, producing every cell in the offspring's body with the mutation, and potentially many organisms in the population are affected. A somatic mutation, on the other hand, starts in one body cell, so only a patch of cells (within that organism) is affected and it is not inherited.

questions.question: Explain how mutations of genes which repair DNA might cause metastatic prostate cancer.
questions.answer: Errors in DNA repair genes can lead to failure to repair mistakes made during DNA replication. This allows mutations to accumulate in a cell in the prostate and results in uncontrollable cell proliferation, that is, cancer (which can then spread).

questions.question: Recent research has suggested that a diet high in processed meats correlates to a higher incidence of prostate cancer. Assess whether consuming processed meats has any scientific basis in causing prostate cancer.
questions.answer: Processed meats are high in carcinogens/mutagens, which are chemicals that can cause mutations in the DNA of cells exposed to them. A diet high in processed meats means these chemicals can accumulate in the prostate gland, increasing the chances of mutations occurring in prostate cells (including in genes that control the cell cycle and DNA repair), which can lead to cancer. Therefore there is a scientific basis for a causal link, although a correlation alone does not prove causation and other factors would also need to be considered.

questions.question: Genetic technologies such as DNA sequencing and DNA profiling can be used to determine inheritance patterns in a population. Compare the results obtained from these two technologies and discuss how they can be used to predict inheritance patterns and the spread of diseases.
questions.answer:
**DNA sequencing** determines the exact nucleotide sequence of a whole genome or of a specific DNA fragment/gene (using PCR and fluorescently labelled markers). The results show mutations, new alleles and diseased genes, and are used for medical diagnoses. It is more expensive but gives complete information. Examples: finding mutations in BRCA genes (tumour suppressor genes) to predict the likelihood of breast cancer and track mutations through a population; sequencing the genetic material of pathogens to track which serotypes/strains are spreading in a population (e.g. influenza, COVID-19) and designing vaccines for the most numerous strains in an outbreak.

**DNA profiling** uses restriction enzymes and PCR to compare short tandem repeats (STRs) at several loci (microsatellites) that vary between individuals, producing a unique banding pattern. It can collect data on a wide scale and track specific markers through populations and families, e.g. paternity testing and forensics. It is inexpensive. It shows which people are more predisposed to certain diseases (limited to risk factors), e.g. the link between sickle cell anaemia and resistance to malaria.

**Comparison:** sequencing reads the actual base sequence and identifies the cause of a disease (individual gene mutations), whereas profiling only compares patterns of markers and cannot show exactly which gene or mutation is present. Both can be used to predict inheritance patterns in populations: sequencing at a large scale and profiling for tracking markers or relatedness in a smaller scale. Used together they allow the spread of non-infectious genetic diseases and infectious disease to be predicted and monitored, helping targeted screening and public health responses.

questions.question: Cosmetics companies seek Kakadu Plum, or gubinge, found in north-western Australia, for its antioxidant- and nutrient-rich properties. For example, the cosmetics company Red Earth was using Kakadu Plum products to hand out on Qantas flights. The patenting of cloned animals, genetically modified crops and genetic materials such as the breast cancer gene is well publicised, but you can also patent natural products. Discuss the patenting of ingredients taken from Aboriginal Australian cultural and intellectual property.
questions.answer: Arguments against: patenting can fail to credit Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people or protect their rights, even though they have used and understood these plants for thousands of years (the knowledge was gained by Aboriginal people and the ingredients have been used for medicine, food and culture). Large companies may exploit this intellectual property for profit, and patents can limit the access of Aboriginal communities to plants that hold cultural significance and are part of their cultural property. Arguments for: ingredients like Kakadu Plum may have benefits for the wider population (e.g. the plant has medicinal properties), and companies already use these products, so patents and agreements (with Aboriginal protocols such as consent and benefit sharing) could provide economic benefits to Aboriginal communities. Overall, patenting is acceptable only if Aboriginal knowledge holders give consent, are acknowledged, and share the benefits.

questions.question: When a person is bitten by a venomous snake, the snake injects a toxin into the person. Antivenom is injected as treatment. This treatment is an example of passive immunity. Outline how the treatment with antivenom works and explain why it is essential to use passive immunity, rather than active immunity.
questions.answer: Antivenom is a solution of ready-made antibodies (from another animal) which are injected into the person; the antibodies bind to the venom (toxin) antigens and neutralise them. Passive immunity gives immediate protection. Active immunity would be too slow: it takes time for the body to stimulate B-plasma cells to produce the required antibodies (and form memory cells) and this delay might result in the death of the individual.

questions.question: A mixture of venoms from several snakes of the same species is used to make antivenom. Suggest why this makes a more effective antivenom.
questions.answer: Different snakes of the same species produce different venoms (different antigens, due to genetic diversity). A mixture means antibodies are made against all the different antigens, so the antivenom will be effective against the venom of any snake of that species, as it will bind to the different venoms.

questions.question: Antivenom is made by the vaccination of animals. Each animal is initially injected with a small volume of venom. Two weeks later, the animals are injected with a larger volume of venom following the purification of antibodies from the animal's blood plasma. Use your knowledge of the humoral immune response to explain this vaccination programme.
questions.answer: The first, small dose of venom is small enough not to harm the animal but its antigens stimulate the cloning of B-plasma cells, which produce specific antibodies, and B-memory cells are also produced. The larger second dose is given after about two weeks: memory B cells respond rapidly (the secondary response), producing a faster, larger concentration of antibodies. Because the animal has already built up immunity, the larger dose does not harm it. The antibodies are then purified from the animal's blood plasma and used as antivenom.

questions.question: Zika is a RNA virus, which can be spread by the *Aedes* mosquito. Most people infected with Zika experience no or very mild symptoms. An outbreak in South America was accompanied by an increase in the number of babies born with microcephaly. In 2016, concern was expressed by athletes travelling to the Olympics in Brazil. The advice given to anyone travelling to the Olympics was: use insect repellent and wear loose clothing that covers the body; keep windows closed at night and sleep under a mosquito net; avoid areas with poor sanitation and stagnant water. Identify the method of transmission of the Zika virus.
questions.answer: Vector (mosquito) transmission: the Zika virus is spread by the bite of the *Aedes* mosquito.

questions.question: The advice given to Olympic travellers to Brazil to reduce the risk of Zika infection was: use insect repellent and wear loose clothing that covers the body; keep windows closed at night and sleep under a mosquito net; avoid areas with poor sanitation and stagnant water. Outline how the preventative methods described would help reduce the chance of infection with Zika.
questions.answer: Each method prevents transmission of the virus: repellent and clothing covering the body and mosquito nets/closed windows prevent the mosquitoes from biting individuals and so stop the virus entering the person's body fluids; avoiding stagnant water and poor sanitation reduces contact with places where mosquitoes breed, reducing the number of vector mosquitoes (and so the chance of being bitten).

questions.question: The diagram shows how the Zika virus replicates inside a human cell (the virus binds to receptors, releases viral RNA, uses the host cell's replication and protein synthesis, assembles new viral particles in the ER/Golgi and releases them from the cell). With reference to the diagram, suggest why viruses are difficult to treat with drugs.
questions.answer: Viruses are not cellular, so have no metabolic pathways of their own to attack with drugs. They enter and replicate inside the host cell, using the host's cell metabolism (the host's replication and protein synthesis), so drugs cannot target the virus inside the cell without interfering with or damaging the host cell's own processes. Any drug would have to disrupt essential host-cell processes.

questions.question: Zika is an RNA virus which can be spread by the *Aedes* mosquito. Outline why it may be difficult to develop an effective vaccine against the Zika virus.
questions.answer: Viruses have high mutation rates (high antigenic variation), so the surface antigens keep changing and a vaccine would have to be constantly remade; the virus may also be hard to target while inside infected cells, and developing a vaccine can be limited by funding and the need to produce it on a very large (global) scale.

With reference to the diagram, suggest why viruses are difficult to treat with drugs.
prev.answer: Viruses are not cellular, so have no metabolic pathways of their own to attack with drugs. They enter and replicate inside the host cell, using the host's cell metabolism (the host's replication and protein synthesis), so drugs cannot target the virus inside the cell without interfering with or damaging the host cell's own processes. Any drug would have to disrupt essential host-cell processes.

questions.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of vaccination programmes, public health campaigns, pharmaceuticals, and genetic engineering in the prevention of epidemics such as Zika.
questions.answer:
**Vaccination programmes:** vaccines stimulate the production of memory cells so that a later infection is fought off quickly, and if a high proportion of a population is vaccinated, herd immunity prevents the pathogen spreading and so prevents epidemics (e.g. the worldwide smallpox vaccination programme eradicated smallpox). Their effectiveness depends on a vaccine being available and a pathogen with stable antigens, on being well subscribed and on mass immunisation; for a pathogen like Zika, which mutates, vaccine development is difficult.

**Public health campaigns:** informing the population about preventing mosquito bites, mosquito control, and early notification and isolation of cases helps reduce transmission (e.g. the SARS campaign in 2003 led to early reporting of symptoms and isolation). Their effectiveness depends on people understanding the messages and following the guidelines and on local government support; they cannot prevent all transmission by themselves.

**Pharmaceuticals:** antivirals treat infected individuals and may shorten illness, but are less effective at stopping epidemics because they must be taken early, depend on being available and distributed (and affordable in poorer countries), and do not prevent infection of others. Viruses are difficult to target with drugs.

**Genetic engineering:** for example CRISPR/gene drives can be used to modify *Aedes* mosquitoes so they cannot transmit the virus or are sterile, reducing the vector population and so transmission. This has high potential, but is costly to deploy and limited by access, regulation, ethics and ecological risks.

**Judgement:** vaccination programmes (once a vaccine exists) are the most effective at preventing epidemics, with public health campaigns the most accessible and immediate measure; pharmaceuticals are the least effective at preventing epidemics. The most effective approach is a combination of methods, so that the weaknesses of each overlap.

questions.question:
The diagram shows meiosis in three stages: A — the chromosomes in a diploid cell are replicated; B — homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments, then separate in the first division; C — the second division separates the chromatids into four haploid cells.

Identify where genetic variation can occur.
questions.answer: Variation arises in B, through crossing over between homologous chromosomes and their independent assortment in meiosis I, and in C, where chromatids that are no longer identical (after crossing over) separate randomly into the four gametes. Stage A, DNA replication, produces identical copies.
options: A and B
B and C
A and C
A, B and C

questions.question: In animals, gametes can join via either external or internal fertilisation. Which of the following statements about fertilisation is correct?
questions.answer: External fertilisation requires water so that gametes do not dry out and sperm can swim to the eggs, so it suits aquatic animals. Both are sexual processes, and external fertilisation produces far more gametes.
options: External and internal fertilisation are asexual processes.
Internal fertilisation produces offspring that develop outside the parent.
External fertilisation produces fewer gametes than internal fertilisation.
External fertilisation is most appropriate for animals in aquatic environments.

questions.question: Scrapie, a disease which causes severe brain damage in sheep, is caused by prions. What type of macromolecule are prions?
questions.answer: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause normal copies of the protein to misfold, damaging nervous tissue. They contain no nucleic acid.
options: Carbohydrate
Lipid
Nucleic acid
Protein

questions.question:
The diagram shows the sequence of bases in the same section of a gene on the maternal and paternal chromosomes of two individuals. The sequences are identical except at one position (boxed), where a single base pair differs (e.g. G–C on one chromosome and A–T on the other).

Which one of the following statements about such individual variations is true?
questions.answer: These are single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). They occur throughout the genome, mostly in non-coding DNA. In a coding region a SNP might change an amino acid and so the phenotype, but because the genetic code is redundant it may not (a silent change).
options: They only occur in sex chromosomes.
They are unlikely to occur in non-coding sections of DNA.
If they occurred in coding sections, they might affect the phenotype.
If they occurred in coding sections, they would definitely affect the phenotype.

questions.question:
Mallard ducks have a colour pattern controlled by multiple alleles — the mallard allele ($M$), the restricted allele ($M^{R}$) and the dusky allele ($m^{d}$). The dominance hierarchy is $M^{R} > M > m^{d}$.

A male duck with the genotype $M^{R}m^{d}$ is mated with a female with the genotype $Mm^{d}$. What will be the most likely genotypic and phenotypic result of this cross?
questions.answer: Offspring: $M^{R}M$ and $M^{R}m^{d}$ (restricted), $Mm^{d}$ (mallard) and $m^{d}m^{d}$ (dusky) — 4 genotypes and 3 phenotypes.
options: 3 genotypes and 2 phenotypes
3 genotypes and 3 phenotypes
4 genotypes and 3 phenotypes
4 genotypes and 4 phenotypes

questions.question:
Himalayan rabbits are normally white with black ears, nose, feet and tail. The ears, nose, feet and tail have a lower temperature than the rest of the body. However, if a patch of fur is plucked from its back and an ice pack is kept on the plucked patch, the new fur that grows there will be black too.

What is the reason for this?
questions.answer: Every cell has the same genotype. The enzyme needed to make black pigment is temperature-sensitive and only works at lower temperatures, so the environment (temperature) affects the phenotype, not the genotype. *(Option C has been corrected: the original paper said the genes are \"switched off\" at lower temperatures, which made no option correct, and the marking guide accepted no answer.)*
options: The genotype of the white fur is affected by the lower temperatures.
Codominant alleles are both expressed in these cooler areas.
The allele for black pigment production is only expressed (its enzyme is only active) at lower temperatures.
Lower temperatures cause mutations in cells, which then produce black pigment.

questions.question:
The diagram shows translation at a ribosome. The mRNA reads 5′ … UGG AAA UGG AAA GAU UUC AAA UGG UUC AAA … and the tRNA carrying aspartic acid (Asp) is paired with the codon GAU.

Determine the DNA sequence on the template (non-coding) strand for the amino acid "Asp".
questions.answer: The mRNA codon for Asp is GAU. The template DNA strand is complementary to the mRNA (with T instead of U), so it reads CTA. CUA is the tRNA anticodon, and GAT is the coding strand.
options: CUA
CTA
GAT
GAU

questions.question:
Comparing the blood of sheep that had died of anthrax with the blood of healthy sheep, Robert Koch found that the blood of the diseased sheep contained small rod-shaped organisms. This discovery became the first step in Koch's postulates.

What is this first step in Koch's postulates?
questions.answer: Koch's first postulate: the microorganism must be found in every organism with the disease (and not in healthy organisms). Isolating and growing it in pure culture is the second postulate.
options: The organism must be grown in pure culture.
The organism must be seen under the microscope in all organisms.
The microbe causing the disease must be found in each diseased organism.
The microbe causing the disease must be isolated and grown in pure culture.

questions.question:
A study was conducted to investigate the incidence of pathogens on vineyard grapes. An extract of the results:

> Of the vineyards studied, we found that 5% had some cases of blue mould rot (BMR), 9% had black rot (BR), 11% had downy mildew (DM), 13% had powdery mildew (PM) and 23% showed eutypa dieback (ED). There were no visible signs (NVS) of pathogens in 72% of the vineyards studied.

Which of the following graphs best represents these results?
questions.answer: The categories are discrete (different diseases), so a column graph is appropriate. A pie chart is wrong because the percentages add to more than 100% (vineyards could have several diseases), and line graphs are for continuous data.
options: Graph A (pie chart)
Graph B (column graph)
Graph C (line graph)
Graph D (line graph with points)

questions.question:
The table shows the mortality from the major causes of death in Australia in 2021. The data were gathered and averaged from a range of sources, and the numbers have been rounded to the nearest hundred.

| Females — disease | Number of deaths | Males — disease | Number of deaths |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dementia/Alzheimer's disease | 9500 | Coronary heart disease | 11 000 |
| Coronary heart disease | 6700 | Dementia/Alzheimer's disease | 5600 |
| Cardiovascular disease | 5800 | Lung cancer | 4600 |
| Lung cancer | 3400 | Cardiovascular disease | 4100 |
| Breast cancer | 3200 | Prostate cancer | 3700 |

Which statement could be made about the data?
questions.answer: Coronary heart disease caused $6700 + 11\,000 = 17\,700$ deaths, more than dementia/Alzheimer's ($9500 + 5600 = 15\,100$), so it was the leading cause overall. (The marking guidelines also accepted D, since the leading causes differ between men and women.)
options: The data is not useful because it is not current.
Overall, coronary heart disease was the leading cause of death in 2021.
The data is not useful because it was gathered from a range of sources.
It is useful to compare the mortality rates of men and women separately.

questions.question:
Yellow fever is a viral disease that is transmitted primarily by mosquitoes. An outbreak of yellow fever was reported in an area of Brazil in January 2017 and was reported to be spreading to other areas within Brazil.

Which one of the following is a correct statement about this outbreak of yellow fever?
questions.answer: Removing breeding sites (standing water) reduces the vector population, so fewer people are bitten and infected. The outbreak is within one country (an epidemic, not a pandemic); infected travellers can be bitten by local mosquitoes and spread it; and outbreaks occur where vaccination rates are low.
options: This outbreak of yellow fever is considered to be a pandemic.
Infected individuals who travel to other areas of Brazil will not increase the spread of the disease.
This outbreak of yellow fever is occurring in populations with high vaccination rates for yellow fever.
Elimination of mosquito breeding sites in areas with yellow fever will reduce the number of individuals affected.
